# FreeITSM Changelog

This file tracks all fixes, improvements, and features for website updates.
Items are logged here and then published to the updates page at freeitsm.co.uk/updates.html.

Each entry has a unique ID (3-digit, sequential) used as `data-id` on the website update items.
When publishing to the website, move entries from **Unpublished** to the **Published** section.

---

## Unpublished



| ID   | Module            | Type        | Description |
|------|-------------------|-------------|-------------|
| 1362 | Contracts        | Improvement | **The whole Contracts module now works on a phone** &mdash; all 22 pages, including the 13-page RFP Builder. The 260px left panel becomes a compact strip: search and **New contract** share a line, the running totals become a row of chips you swipe, and the quick links another. Every list &mdash; contracts, suppliers, contacts, RFPs, uploaded documents and extracted requirements &mdash; becomes a **card per row**, with the column headings printed against the values that would be meaningless without them. Not every table does: a coverage map, a supplier comparison and the two AI cost logs keep their columns and scroll sideways, because you read those **down a column** rather than a row at a time, and a card cannot show you that. Contract and supplier detail pages stop squeezing their paired fields into two columns, and every dialogue in the module fills the screen with 16px fields &mdash; which is not a cosmetic point on iOS, where a smaller field makes Safari zoom and abandon the phone layout entirely. **The desktop is untouched**, provably: every rule is inside a mobile-only block, and the measurements at desktop width are identical before and after. |
| 1363 | Contracts        | Fix         | **The collapsing left panel is no longer a dead end on a phone.** Contracts lets each analyst set the left panel to appear **on hover**, which stores it as a 16px strip that opens when you point at it. A phone has nothing to point with, so anybody using that setting had the search box, the totals, the quick links and the **New contract** button sealed inside a strip that could not be opened at all &mdash; on every page of the module. The panel now always opens on a small screen, whichever setting you use, and the choice keeps working exactly as before on a desktop. |
| 1364 | Contracts        | Fix         | **A contract&rsquo;s own title was being squeezed off its page.** On a narrow screen the five buttons at the top of a contract (Back, Task, Calendar, Equipment report, Edit) refused to give way, leaving about 130px for the heading &mdash; so a contract number broke across two lines, its title across three, and the last button ran off the edge where it could not be tapped. The heading now takes the full width and the buttons wrap beneath it. The same fault sat on nine RFP Builder pages under a different name and is fixed with it. |
| 1365 | Contracts        | Fix         | **The printable equipment report fits a phone.** Its six-column table ran off the side of the screen with no way to reach the last three columns; it now scrolls within the page and the Print and Back buttons are large enough to hit. Printing is unaffected &mdash; the change cannot apply to paper &mdash; and neither is the emailed copy of the same report, which is deliberately left alone because email clients cannot be relied on to honour these rules. |
| 1366 | Contracts        | Improvement | **The Contracts strip on a phone is less crowded.** The row of links to Suppliers, Contacts, RFP Builder and Settings is gone &mdash; every one of them is already in the menu behind the ☰ button, so it was a second copy of the same navigation taking a row of a small screen. The RFP Builder keeps its own **user guide** link, which is the one entry that is genuinely not in that menu. **Search** and **New contract** gained room to breathe: they had been sitting flush against the edge of the screen and against each other, which turns out not to have been a styling choice at all but a leftover from the collapsing left panel &mdash; see the next entry. Requested by Ed. |
| 1367 | Contracts        | Fix         | **The collapsing left panel was flattening the phone layout as well as hiding it.** Fixing the *hover* left-panel setting for small screens (#1363) restored the panel but not its spacing, because the collapsed 16px rail sets its padding to nothing and that instruction outranked the one meant to replace it. The result was a strip whose contents were pressed against both edges of the screen for anyone using that setting. |
| 1368 | Contracts        | Improvement | **The running totals are now a small dashboard.** Contracts, Active, Expiring, Suppliers and Contacts had been a single row of chips that ran off the side of a phone &mdash; so **Expiring**, the one figure most people open Contracts to check, was behind a sideways swipe. They are now cards, two to a row, with the number above its caption and an amber spine on the one that is a warning. It also makes the module consistent with itself: the RFP Builder already presented its own totals exactly this way two taps further in. Suggested by Ed. |
| 1369 | Contracts        | Improvement | **A contract&rsquo;s actions sit along the bottom of a phone screen.** Back, Task, Calendar, Equipment report and Edit become icons in a bar pinned to the bottom, where a thumb already is &mdash; the same treatment knowledge articles and the ticket reading pane already use. That gives the contract number and title the full width of the screen back, and each icon keeps a spoken name for screen readers. Requested by Ed. |
| 1370 | Contracts        | Fix         | **Save and Cancel now sit at the very bottom of the edit screen.** They stopped about 27px short, so the page showed through in a strip underneath them, and on a narrow screen the bar also hung off both edges. Two separate causes: the bar was pinned in a way that cannot reach past the bottom of the box it lives in, and it was stretching itself to fit a wider margin than the page now uses. |
| 1371 | Contracts        | Fix         | **Bullet points in a contract&rsquo;s terms no longer sit outside the panel.** Lists written into the **Terms detail** tabs lost their indentation to an app-wide styling reset, which left the bullets themselves drawn to the left of the text and, on a phone, on the edge of the panel. Numbered lists were affected the same way. **The desktop screen is deliberately untouched** &mdash; it has enough padding that the markers sit inside it and nothing looks wrong. Spotted by Ed. |
| 1372 | Contracts        | Improvement | **The contract terms editor has a full-screen button.** A page of terms and conditions in a 300px-tall box is hard work on a desktop and most of the screen on a phone. The button is the **first** control on the toolbar rather than the last, deliberately: on a narrow screen the toolbar collapses into a menu, and the one control that rescues a small editor should not be the one hidden inside it. |
| 1373 | Contracts        | Fix         | **Switches in the contract form are visible in dark mode again.** **Personal data transferred** and **DPIA required** appeared as two white dots with nothing around them, and only looked like switches once you had tapped one &mdash; so there was no way to tell an unset one from a control that had failed to draw. The track had been given a *surface* colour, which by definition matches the panel behind it; every other switch in FreeITSM uses a fixed grey for exactly this reason. This one is corrected **everywhere rather than only on a phone**, because the same near-invisible track was there in light mode and on the desktop too &mdash; it just showed up first in the dark. Spotted by Ed. |
| 1374 | System           | Fix         | **The confirmation box for removing an attached document was empty.** Taking a document off any record &mdash; a contract, a supplier, an asset, a ticket &mdash; asked you to confirm in a dialogue that showed a heading, an **OK** and a **Cancel** and no question, so there was nothing to say what was about to be removed. The message was being prepared correctly and then passed to the dialogue in a form it does not read. It now names the document, as it was always meant to. Spotted by Ed on the contracts screen; it affected every record type that can hold documents. |
| 1375 | Contracts        | Improvement | **A contract gets the whole phone screen.** Opening or editing one still showed the **New contract** button and the five running totals above it &mdash; 279px of a 740px screen, leaving 411px for the contract itself. Those totals are orientation: they tell you where you are *before* you have chosen a record, and once you are inside one they are describing a list you have already left. They now appear on the list screens only, and a contract, a supplier or an edit form fills the display. Nothing is lost &mdash; **Back** is the first control in the bar along the bottom, and the menu button is where it always was. Requested by Ed. |
| 1376 | Contracts        | Feature     | **Suppliers and Contacts each have two views on a phone: Overview and a directory.** **Overview** is the figures &mdash; how many suppliers in total, then a breakdown by type and status (or, for contacts, by the supplier they work for). The **directory** drops all of that, gives the list the entire screen, and puts a **search box along the bottom** that filters just that list &mdash; suppliers on the suppliers screen, contacts on the contacts screen &mdash; rather than searching the whole module. It matches as you type across every column shown, so a city or a job title finds a record as readily as a name, and says so plainly when nothing matches. Each visit opens on Overview. **The desktop is unchanged in every respect** &mdash; the switch and the search box are not built at all on a wide screen. Requested by Ed. |
| 1377 | Contracts        | Improvement | **Searching contracts opens a full screen.** It had been a floating panel with the page showing round three of its edges, which on a dark theme left an amber bar, a dark panel and a dark page running together &mdash; Ed&apos;s description was &ldquo;a sea of yellow and black without clear borders&rdquo;. It now fills the display, and each result is a bordered card carrying its type, its title and the supplier or owner beneath, so the list reads as a list. The results previously separated themselves only by a hover tint, which a touch screen never shows. **The same full-screen treatment reaches the search boxes in Tickets, Problem Management and Change Management**, which share this component and had the identical problem. |
| 1378 | Contracts        | Fix         | **Adding equipment to a contract uses the whole screen.** The panel listing the assets you can attach was fixed at 320px tall &mdash; sized for a small dialogue on a desktop, and barely half the height of a phone, so you scrolled a short window inside a mostly empty screen. It now grows to fill whatever room the dialogue has, and the rows are large enough to hit. |
| 1379 | System           | Fix         | **Three settings screens started a fifth of a screen too low.** Contracts, Asset Management and Service Status left a 30px gap above their tab strip on a phone that the other eleven settings screens did not, because each carried a margin of its own that the shared mobile layer never overrode. Fixed for all three at once. Contracts&apos; settings tables were checked against the same rules at the same time and were already correct: every one keeps its column headings and scrolls sideways, which is how every settings table in FreeITSM behaves. |
| 1380 | Contracts        | Fix         | **Consolidated requirements are readable on a phone.** The type and priority pills, the requirement itself and its three buttons all shared one row that refused to wrap, and everything except the requirement held its width &mdash; so the sentence people are actually reading got **104px, and ran 801px down the screen**, two or three words to a line. The pills now take a row of their own and the requirement uses the full width beneath them, with the AI&apos;s reasoning under that. Reported by Ed. |
| 1381 | Contracts        | Fix         | **Edit, Split and Delete on a consolidated requirement were invisible on a phone.** They only appeared when the pointer was over the row, and a touch screen has no pointer &mdash; so the three buttons took up space on every row, pushing the text narrower still, while never once being visible to tap on purpose. They now show as a row of full-width buttons underneath the requirement they act on. |
| 1382 | Contracts        | Improvement | **Editing a requirement is laid out properly on a phone.** **Type**, **Priority** and **Category** shared a single row of three, and because each column sized itself to its own longest option rather than to a third of the space, they came out 133px, 101px and 74px wide &mdash; which is why it read as squished at random rather than merely tight. A 74px dropdown cannot show a category name. Each now has a row to itself at the full width of the screen, the requirement box is given the room a full-screen sheet has, and **Cancel** and **Save** sit along the bottom. The desktop dialogue is unchanged. Reported by Ed. |
| 1383 | Contracts        | Fix         | **Editing an extracted requirement is laid out properly on a phone.** Every field started in a different place and had a different width &mdash; the requirement box 230px and indented 114px, the type dropdown 287px indented 57px, the source quote 158px indented 186px &mdash; because each field&apos;s **label was sitting beside it rather than above it**, pushing it in by however long that label happened to be. The page is written for stacked labels; a shared stylesheet was quietly turning each row into a side-by-side pair. Labels now sit above their fields, every field is the full width of the screen, and the requirement box has the room a full-screen sheet gives it. The document details along the top wrap instead of running off the edge. Reported by Ed. |
| 1384 | Contracts        | Fix         | **The Delete button on an uploaded RFP document has never worked.** Tapping it did nothing at all &mdash; no confirmation, no error, no clue. The document&apos;s filename was being written into the button&apos;s own click handler still wrapped in quotation marks, which ended the handler early and left it as a fragment the browser could not run; every press raised a silent parse error. It now asks for confirmation, naming the file, and deletes as intended. **This was broken on the desktop too**, for every document, since the page was written. Reported by Ed. |
| 1385 | Contracts        | Improvement | **Re-running text extraction on a document now says that it worked.** The button did its job every time &mdash; it just did it in total silence, and on a document that already had text the row it refreshed looked identical, so it read as a dead control. It now confirms with the number of characters read, in a message that appears wherever you are on the page rather than beside the upload box at the top. Reported by Ed. |
| 1386 | Contracts        | Fix         | **Section cards on a generated RFP document were unreadable on a phone.** The heading, the description, the requirement count, the version and the generated time were all rendering in an **11-pixel-wide column** &mdash; roughly one character per line, running 480px down the screen &mdash; because the three buttons beside them refused to give up any width. The text now takes the full width of the card and the buttons sit on a row of their own beneath it. Reported by Ed. |
| 1387 | Contracts        | Improvement | **The procurement context note fills the screen on a phone.** The box was a fixed six rows &mdash; sized for a desktop dialogue &mdash; floating in a sheet nearly four times its height, and the heading, the explanation and the box itself ran into one another with no space between them. The note now grows to use the whole sheet, and the three parts are separated. Requested by Ed. |
| 1388 | System           | Fix         | **Rich-text editors no longer zoom the page when you tap into them on an iPhone.** iOS Safari zooms in on any field whose text is smaller than 16px, and in a full-screen editor that does more than look untidy: the zoom pushes the page wider than the screen, Safari re-lays it out at desktop width, and **the entire mobile layout switches off** until you reload. The editor&apos;s text is now 16px on touch devices and stays exactly as it was on a desktop, where there is nothing to zoom. Reported by Ed on the RFP section editor; the same fault was found in **six of the eleven rich-text editors in FreeITSM** and all six are fixed &mdash; including Change Management, Tasks and two on the ticket settings screen, which are already mobile-friendly in every other respect. |
| 1389 | Portal           | Fix         | **The description box on the portal&apos;s new-ticket form was a stub in the top-right corner.** On a normal desktop screen the box you type your problem into was about 300px wide and 62px tall, tucked into the corner, while the mailbox and priority menus below it had the full width. The message area and the settings panel sit in a two-column layout, and a **third item &mdash; the *Description* label &mdash; had been added to it**, so the browser filled the next free cell with each item in turn: the label took the wide column, the editor was pushed into the narrow one meant for the settings panel, and the settings dropped to the row beneath. The editor now fills the left-hand side at the full height of the page and everything you merely *set* &mdash; mailbox, priority, equipment, attachments &mdash; sits in the panel on the right. **A phone was never affected**: below 900px the layout is a single column, where all three stack in order, which is why this survived. Reported by tjedelhauser in [#122](https://github.com/edmozley/freeitsm/issues/122). |
| 1390 | Portal           | Fix         | **The description box collapsed to a sliver on a tablet.** Between 769px and 900px wide &mdash; where a tablet held upright lands &mdash; the message area had no minimum height of its own, so it shrank to about 49px: a toolbar with a sliver underneath and nowhere obvious to type. The rule that prevents this existed and was correct, but had been written for screens up to 768px while the single-column layout it was correcting starts at 900px, so a band of widths in between was left uncovered. |
| 1391 | Workflows        | Fix         | **The "Add a note to the ticket" workflow action has never worked.** Every time it ran it failed with `Column 'analyst_id' cannot be null`, on every installation, since the action was written. The engine sets that column to nothing **on purpose** &mdash; it is how an entry is marked as written by automation rather than by a person &mdash; but the column had never been told to allow it. Ticket history now accepts an entry that nobody made, and such entries are shown as **System** rather than the previous &ldquo;Unknown&rdquo;, which said *we do not know* when the truth was *nobody did it*. **Existing installations pick this up by running System &rarr; Database Verification**, which reports the change in plain English; new ones get it from the schema. Nothing else changes: every entry a person makes is unaffected, and both screens that read ticket history already coped with an entry having no author. Reported by Kraleemil in [#120](https://github.com/edmozley/freeitsm/issues/120). |
| 1392 | LMS              | Improvement | **The LMS works on a phone.** All six screens &mdash; the courses console, My courses, the course editor, the player, the guide and settings. The console&apos;s four tables are handled differently because they are different things: courses, groups and assignments become **a card per row** (a group&apos;s description is a sentence, and a sentence cannot be read sideways), while the **progress report keeps its columns and scrolls**, because it is read down the Status and Score columns across people and seven columns cannot be carried by reading order. Column headings that a value cannot do without &mdash; an upload date, a member count, a deadline &mdash; are printed against the value, taken from the table&apos;s own translated headings rather than written again. **The desktop is untouched.** |
| 1393 | LMS              | Fix         | **The course contents and the lesson list were deleted on smaller screens, with nothing in their place.** Below 900px the player&apos;s table of contents and the editor&apos;s lesson list &mdash; which is also where **Add lesson** lives &mdash; were simply hidden. Both are the main way to move around, so a course could only be paged through one lesson at a time with no sense of where you were, and the editor could not add a lesson at all. Both now open as a panel from a button, over the page, closing when you pick something. |
| 1394 | LMS              | Fix         | **A tablet held upright lost the course contents entirely.** The rule that hid those panels started at 900px while the replacement panel starts at 768px, so every width in between had the contents removed and no button to bring them back &mdash; the first change had happened and the second had not. The two now share a breakpoint: above it you get the real sidebar, below it the panel. |
| 1395 | LMS              | Fix         | **Deleting a lesson was impossible on a touch screen.** The delete button on each lesson in the course editor only appeared when a mouse pointer was over its row, and a touch screen has no pointer &mdash; so the button took up space on every row while never once being visible to tap on purpose. |
| 1396 | LMS              | Fix         | **Course names sat too close to the edge of their card on a phone.** The list rows had 4px of padding where every other card feed in FreeITSM uses 14px, so the LMS was the one module crowding its own panel. It now matches the rest. Spotted by Ed. |
| 1397 | LMS              | Fix         | **The buttons at the bottom of a lesson sat underneath Safari&apos;s address bar.** The three LMS screens sized themselves to the full height of the window as if the browser had no toolbars, so anything pinned to the bottom was drawn behind them. They now take the height actually available, and the bar clears the home indicator on phones that have one. Reported by Ed. |
| 1398 | LMS              | Fix         | **The lesson editor was sometimes empty until you reloaded the page.** The editor and the lesson content were being fetched at the same time, and whichever finished second decided the outcome: if the content arrived first, it was written to an editor that did not exist yet and **silently discarded**. Reloading simply ran the race again and usually won. The content is now held until the editor is ready, so the order no longer matters. This happened on a desktop too &mdash; a slower phone just lost the race more often. Reported by Ed. |
| 1399 | LMS              | Improvement | **Editing a lesson on a phone is now two pages rather than one long scroll.** A switch at the top moves between the **lesson text** and its **questions**, so you no longer scroll past an entire rich-text editor to reach the questions and back again to save. The first tab is named after the lesson itself, which is also the only place a phone says which lesson you are editing. **Course settings**, **Preview** and **AI: write this lesson** are gathered into a bar along the bottom, and the editor&apos;s **full-screen** button is moved to the front of its toolbar &mdash; it was already there, but at phone width it was collapsing into the overflow menu, which is exactly where the control that rescues a small editor should not be. The desktop editor is unchanged. Requested by Ed. |
| 1400 | LMS              | Improvement | **The questions page of a lesson now puts its heading on its own line.** On a phone the **Questions** heading was sharing a row with **AI: write questions** and **+ Add question**, three things across the width of a handset. The heading now sits on its own line with the two buttons below it, sharing the width evenly and tall enough to tap. The separator line that divides the questions from the editor above them is also dropped on that page, where it was dividing the heading from nothing. Desktop is unchanged. Requested by Ed. |
| 1401 | LMS              | Improvement | **The Progress screen no longer scrolls sideways on a phone.** It was a wide table you dragged left and right to reach the status and score columns; each row is now a card, with the analyst as its heading, the status beside the name, and the course, group, score, deadline and last access labelled underneath. The **view** button sits in the card&apos;s bottom-right corner rather than taking a row of its own. Requested by Ed. |
| 1402 | LMS              | Improvement | **The three Progress filters are behind one button on a phone.** Course, group, analyst and status stacked into four full-width rows and spent most of the screen before a single result. They now open as a full-screen sheet from a filter icon on a bar along the bottom. The desktop keeps all four on one line as before. Requested by Ed. |
| 1403 | LMS              | Fix         | **The LMS console could not be scrolled at all on a phone.** Anything below the fold on the Courses, Groups, Assignments and Progress tabs was unreachable &mdash; the page filled the screen exactly and nothing would move. The list area is now the scrolling region, as it is in every other module. Reported by Ed. |
| 1404 | LMS              | Improvement | **The demo data now fills the Progress tab.** Importing the LMS demo module gave you two courses and their lessons, but no learning groups, no assignments and no progress &mdash; so the Progress tab, which is where a manager spends their time, was empty on a fresh install. It now creates two groups (**All staff** and **New starters**), assigns a course to each, and records progress covering every state the screen can show, including one that is overdue. |
| 1405 | LMS              | Feature     | **Progress can be filtered by analyst.** A fourth filter sits alongside course, group and status, and lists only the people the current course and group selection actually covers. It combines with the others rather than replacing them, so you can ask for one person on one course. Requested by Ed. |
| 1406 | LMS              | Fix         | **An overdue row was unreadable on a phone in a dark theme.** The pale pink that marks an overdue row on a desktop table became a near-white card filling the width of the screen, with the theme&apos;s own light text on it. On a phone the card now carries a red edge instead, so it stands out without any of its own colours changing. The desktop table is unchanged. |
| 1407 | LMS              | Improvement | **Preview in the course editor now brings you back to the editor.** It opens the real learner player, and the player&apos;s back button went to the course list &mdash; three clicks from the lesson you had been editing. Coming from the editor, it now returns there. Reported by Ed. |
| 1408 | LMS              | Fix         | **The lessons panel stayed open on top of what you had just asked for.** On a phone, opening the lessons panel in the course editor and tapping **AI: draft an outline** left the panel covering the dialogue it had opened. Both of the panel&apos;s buttons now close it, the same way choosing a lesson already did. Reported by Ed. |
| 1409 | LMS              | Fix         | **The course editor claimed there were unsaved changes when there were none.** Moving between AI-drafted lessons asked whether you wanted to discard changes you had never made. The editor was comparing the lesson as stored against the editor&apos;s own re-formatted copy of it, and TinyMCE rewrites characters such as an em dash into HTML entities &mdash; so any lesson whose text had not itself been typed into the editor looked modified the moment it opened. AI drafts hit this every time, because they are written straight to the database and use real dashes and quotes. The comparison is now taken from the editor on both sides. Reported by Ed. |
| 1410 | LMS              | Fix         | **The editor&apos;s full-screen button only went full width, not full screen.** On a phone the editor stretched across the screen but stayed a fifth of its height, because the rule that sizes it inside the lesson page was overriding the one the full-screen mode sets. It now fills the whole screen, and the tab strip and bottom bar step out of the way while it does. Reported by Ed. |
| 1411 | Tickets          | Feature     | **A mailbox can use a different login for sending than for reading.** Plenty of providers issue separate SMTP credentials, and until now FreeITSM always sent with the IMAP username and password. The mailbox dialogue now asks the question the way an online checkout asks about a billing address: a switch that says **Use the IMAP login for sending**, on by default, with a username and password appearing underneath when you turn it off. Existing mailboxes are unaffected and keep sending exactly as before. Both new fields are encrypted at rest, and **Database Verification adds the columns** on an existing installation. Suggested and prototyped by **Kraleemil** in [#119](https://github.com/edmozley/freeitsm/pull/119). |
| 1412 | Workflow         | Fix         | **A workflow that sent an email from a basic IMAP mailbox always failed.** The **Send email** action knew how to talk to Microsoft and Google but not to a plain SMTP server, so it asked for an access token that a basic mailbox can never have and stopped with *"Failed to obtain a valid access token"* &mdash; an error pointing at OAuth, on a mailbox that does not use it. Found by **Kraleemil** while working on [#119](https://github.com/edmozley/freeitsm/pull/119). |
| 1413 | System           | Fix         | **Database Verification could not create two of the knowledge-gap tables.** Every run reported *"Key column &apos;id&apos; doesn&apos;t exist in table"* for `knowledge_gap_tickets` and `knowledge_gap_cluster_tickets`. Neither has an `id` column &mdash; one is keyed by its ticket, the other by a pair of columns &mdash; and the table builder assumed every table has one. Composite and non-`id` keys are now declared in a single list rather than half in a list and half in the builder, so adding a table like this is one line in one place. Reported by **chris18890** in [#123](https://github.com/edmozley/freeitsm/issues/123). |
| 1414 | System           | Fix         | **A brand-new installation still had the workflow-note bug that was fixed in #1391.** Verification declares the database schema in three places and #1391 only updated two, so a fresh install created `ticket_audit.analyst_id` as **NOT NULL** &mdash; and a workflow adding a note to a ticket failed again with *"Column &apos;analyst_id&apos; cannot be null"* until Database Verification was run a second time. An existing installation was never affected. The third declaration now matches the other two, which is also what the verification screen was warning about. Reported by **chris18890** in [#123](https://github.com/edmozley/freeitsm/issues/123) and confirmed by Ed. |
| 1415 | Process Mapper   | Improvement | **The Process Mapper works on a phone &mdash; for reading a map.** All three of its screens now fit a phone: the process list opens as a slide-in panel instead of taking 72% of the width, the toolbar scrolls sideways rather than pushing the page off the edge, the export dialogue fills the screen, and the step-types settings table becomes a card feed with its column headings kept. A map itself pans with a finger. **Building** a map still needs a mouse &mdash; steps are moved by dragging and their actions live behind a right-click, neither of which a touch screen has &mdash; so that is left as it was rather than half-wired. |
| 1416 | Process Mapper   | Fix         | **With the left panel set to &quot;show on hover&quot;, the process list could not be opened on a phone at all.** That preference collapses the list to a 16px strip that expands when the mouse approaches, and a touch screen never hovers &mdash; so every process map in the system sat behind a control that a finger cannot operate. The preference is untouched on a desktop; on a phone the list is reached by a button instead. Found on Ed&apos;s own account, which had the preference set. |
| 1417 | Process Mapper   | Fix         | **The process list was laid out by another module&apos;s rules.** Problem Management and Process Mapper both use `pm-` for their class names, and one of Problem Management&apos;s phone rules is not scoped to it &mdash; so it arranged the Process Mapper panel into two columns and squeezed every process name down to a letter or two (&quot;S&hellip;&quot;, &quot;I&hellip;&quot;). Problem Management is unaffected and unchanged. |
| 1418 | Process Mapper   | Improvement | **Tapping a box on a phone opens its details as a panel along the bottom.** Tapping a step, group or lane already selected it; its details panel is a 320px column down the right-hand side, which on a phone left almost no map. It now rises from the bottom and takes a little over half the screen, with the label, type, colour and description editable as normal. **The map stays visible above it, and the item you tapped is scrolled into that space** so you can see what you are editing. The desktop panel is unchanged. Ed&apos;s idea. |
| 1419 | Process Mapper   | Fix         | **The Left panel tab in settings did nothing.** Clicking it raised a JavaScript error and the tab never changed, on a desktop as much as on a phone &mdash; it has never worked. The tab strip calls a function by name, and this screen was the only settings screen whose tab switcher was tucked away where that call could not reach it. Reported by Ed. |

| 1432 | Tickets          | Feature     | **A message that has arrived before says so.** A long ticket is more often the same message five times than one long message &mdash; a resend, a distribution list delivering twice, a bounce carrying the original back, an auto-reply quoting the lot. It can refresh itself once the conversation has moved a set number of messages ahead, and only when somebody actually opens the ticket, so a queue nobody is reading never costs anything. **Off until you turn it on**, under **Tickets &rarr; Settings &rarr; General**, with four settings: whether to have it, when to refresh, how far back to read, and whether it may read internal notes. | 1434 | Tickets          | Feature     | **&quot;Read it for me&quot; &mdash; a briefing on a ticket you have never seen.** A different question from the standing summary: the short version, how it got here, what is unresolved, and what it would do next. It is **required to separate what the ticket says from what it is inferring**, and to head its suggestions with *These are suggestions, not conclusions*, because the failure mode here is somebody acting on a confident guess. **Nothing is stored** &mdash; you ask for it, you read it, it is gone &mdash; so it can never become a fact the next person reads without knowing a machine wrote it. | 1437 | Tickets          | Fix         | **Clicking &quot;Read it for me&quot; twice charged you twice.** With nothing on screen but a motionless *Reading the ticket…* for a minute, clicking again is the natural thing to do &mdash; and every click was a fresh paid call, with the second answer overwriting the first. | 1438 | System           | Feature     | **System &rarr; AI thinking &mdash; one switch per AI feature, and everything got faster.** Some models *think at length* before they answer: they spend their whole output budget reasoning before writing a character, and you pay for every token of it. Every AI feature in FreeITSM summarises, extracts or drafts from text already in front of it; none of them is a puzzle, which is what extended thinking is for. So it is now **off unless you ask for it**, feature by feature, on a new **System &rarr; AI thinking** page that shows all nine with the provider and model each is using. | 1444 | Tickets          | Fix         | **Notes were stamped with the server&#39;s clock instead of UTC, so they read into the future.** A note added to a ticket showed a time ahead of the one it was written at &mdash; two hours ahead on a server set to Vienna, one hour in the UK in summer, and exactly right on a server running UTC, which is why it lasted. Everything else on the ticket was correct, and that contrast was the diagnosis: every other datetime is written with `UTC_TIMESTAMP()`, but the note insert **did not name its date column at all**, so the column&#39;s own `DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP` filled it in &mdash; and MySQL evaluates that in the connection&#39;s session timezone, which is the server&#39;s own clock. The reader then converts it as if it were UTC, and the note lands the server&#39;s offset into the future. The answer was already two lines below the fault: the same method updates the ticket with `UTC_TIMESTAMP()` in the same transaction. **Notes added by the four other routes were never affected** &mdash; a merge summary, an AI summary, an integration comment and a sent attachment all named the column. ⚠️ **Existing notes are not corrected**: the table holds rows from both routes and nothing records which wrote which, so a migration would have to guess, and it would move the ones that were already right. Reported by **mbsouth** in [#126](https://github.com/edmozley/freeitsm/issues/126). |

| 1306 | Tasks             | Feature     | **Tasks can now repeat.** A task can be set to come back daily, weekly, monthly or yearly, every so many of them, and the patterns go well beyond that: particular weekdays ("every second week on Monday and Thursday"), a day of the month including the last day whatever its length, or a named weekday within the month such as the third Monday or the last Friday. A repeat can run forever, stop on a date, or stop after a set number of occurrences. There are two ways to repeat and the difference matters: **after completion**, where the next one appears when you finish the last and is counted from the day you actually did it, which is what most people mean by a monthly check; or **on a fixed schedule**, where occurrences arrive on their dates whether or not the previous one was finished, which is what a compliance review needs. Each new occurrence can carry forward the description, subtasks, assignees, tags, links to tickets and changes, and attached documents, each of those chosen separately &mdash; carrying the attachments is right for a checklist and wrong for an audit that gathers fresh evidence each time. A new occurrence always arrives open and unfinished, never in the status the previous one was closed into. Fixed schedules catch up on anything missed while a server was down rather than quietly skipping it, and cannot produce the same occurrence twice however often the background job runs. Requested by dschipfel in discussion #94. |

The calendar gains a **Show** control: tasks only, as before; tasks and subtasks together; or subtasks on their own. Subtasks are drawn in the same colour as everything else, because colour already carries status and priority and has to go on meaning that, and are marked with a dashed edge instead. The day view names the task a subtask belongs to and the month view carries it in the tooltip, since a subtask called "Rack it" rarely says on its own which piece of work it is part of. Requested by dschipfel in discussion #90. |
| 1302 | Authentication    | Improvement | **Analysts who also have a self-service account can now jump straight to the portal from their account menu.** The two are separate logins with separate accounts, so the entry only appears for an analyst who actually has a portal account they could sign in to &mdash; on a typical installation most analysts do not, and offering everyone the link would simply have dropped them on a sign-in page asking for credentials they have never had. | 1300 | Authentication    | Improvement | **The analyst sign-in page now offers a way across to the self-service portal.** The portal's own sign-in page has carried a link to the analyst page since it was built, but the link only went one way, so somebody who followed a bookmark or an emailed link to the wrong one of the two had no route across except editing the address bar. Requested by dschipfel in discussion #82. |
| 1299 | System            | Feature     | **FreeITSM is now available in Danish, completely.** It joins as the twenty-fifth language, chosen because a Danish installation reported two faults in a week and had been reading English messages throughout while doing it. Every module is covered &mdash; all twenty-four sections, close to eleven thousand pieces of text, from the ticket list and its settings through assets, the CMDB, contracts and the request-for-proposal builder to the in-product help pages. At the time of writing that makes Danish the most complete translation FreeITSM has, marginally ahead of German. Nothing was seeded from Norwegian: the two languages are close enough that a machine-assisted copy would look convincing and be wrong in precisely the vocabulary software uses. Danish conventions are followed rather than English ones carried across &mdash; lower-case month and weekday names, abbreviations that take a full stop, the informal address Danish software uses, and the Danish terms Microsoft's own products use where a screen refers to them. A pass was also made across module boundaries to settle places where the same English word had been given two different Danish renderings, which matters most for things like the first tab of every help page, previously named one thing in seven modules and another in nine. A note in the language registry that discouraged incremental translation was corrected along the way: it claimed a partly translated language would break the modules it had not reached, which was never true of a section that is simply absent. |
| 1298 | Authentication    | Fix         | **The same permanent sign-in lock-out existed in the directory path.** Sweeping for other instances of #1296 found LDAP and Active Directory sign-in resolving a person exactly the same way &mdash; by the directory identity first &mdash; and dead-ending in the same manner when the account behind that link had been deleted: an analyst was told their account was inactive when it did not exist at all, and a portal user was told theirs could not be found, with no route back for either. The link is now cleared and the sign-in continues down the ordinary path, as it does for single sign-on. The handling moved to one shared place so the two sign-in routes cannot drift apart again. Worth noting for anyone reading the code: the directory path re-links inside a block that deliberately ignores its own failure, so without clearing the stale link the person would sign in while the link stayed pointing at the deleted record indefinitely, with nothing reporting it. |
| 1297 | System            | Fix         | **Importing demo data deleted real accounts.** The importer cleared each table it was about to populate before inserting, and because nothing distinguished a sample row from a real one it cleared the whole table. Importing Core therefore emptied the analysts table apart from a single hardcoded exemption for `admin`, emptied the users table outright, and took departments, teams, RBAC roles and their capability rows with it &mdash; on a live installation, with no confirmation on a first import and a warning that only said conflicts "may" occur. Every row the importer creates is now marked as demo data, and only rows carrying that mark are removed, so a re-import replaces its own sample records and leaves everything else untouched. The clearing step also no longer disables foreign key checks, which is what had been stranding rows that pointed at the deleted records (see #1296); if something outside a module still refers to its demo data the import now stops, names what is in the way, and changes nothing. The page asks before every import rather than only before a repeat one, says what will actually happen, and works out which modules have demo data by counting marked rows instead of asking whether a table has any rows at all &mdash; which had been reporting real tickets and real assets as demo data. Installations that imported demo data before it was marked cannot have it recognised retrospectively, and are now told so rather than quietly ending up with two copies &mdash; including when the import stops because of it, which previously reported a raw database error naming a record the administrator never created. |
| 1296 | Authentication    | Fix         | **A single sign-on account could be locked out permanently, and re-creating it by hand did not help.** Signing in resolves a person by their identity provider's subject claim first, and that lookup was treated as proof the account still existed. If the account had been deleted while the link to it survived, the sign-in committed to the "returning user" path and dead-ended there &mdash; email matching and just-in-time provisioning both sit in the branch past it, so a person whose account had gone could never be re-created, and an administrator re-adding them with the same address changed nothing because the stale link still pointed at the old record. Both identity tables cascade correctly when an account is deleted through the interface, which is why this only surfaced via the demo data importer, which deletes with foreign key checks off and so leaves the links behind. A link whose account no longer exists is now cleared and the sign-in continues down the ordinary first-time path, with the same verified-email and provider checks. Reported by the same person as issue #117. |
| 1295 | Change Management  | Fix         | **A change could be created with a status nobody is allowed to choose.** The change module picks its starting type, status, priority and impact by looking for the row marked as the default, and that lookup did not check whether the row was still active. Deactivating a lookup value removes it from every dropdown but leaves it in the table, so an administrator who retired the default without first promoting another one left new changes being stamped with a value that cannot be selected, edited towards, or reasoned about &mdash; and nothing said so. It now ignores inactive rows and falls back through the display order, so there is always an answer as long as one active row exists. Found while fixing the same shape in Tasks (#1294); the change module never had the more serious half of that fault. |
| 1294 | Tasks              | Fix         | **Setting a different default status or priority for tasks did nothing.** A new task takes its starting status and priority from the module's settings, and the code asked for the row *named* `To Do` and the row *named* `Medium` before it asked which row was marked as the default. On an English install that quietly overruled the administrator: mark High as your default priority and tasks kept arriving as Medium, because the seeded name won the race. On a translated install it did something worse. The name matched nothing, and while there was a fallback here &mdash; so tasks did at least get *a* priority &mdash; this is the identical shape as GH #79, where every ticket intake path looked its starting status up by the word `Open` and a German site that had renamed it to *Offen* got tickets with no status at all and no error. That fix established the rule and this is the sweep that should have gone with it: **the display name belongs to the user, so nothing may be derived from it.** Both lookups now resolve the configured default and nothing else, with inactive rows filtered out rather than merely sorted down &mdash; a deactivated default is absent from the dropdown, so choosing it would reproduce the symptom by another route. A closed status is still allowed to be the default, because an administrator who sets one has said what they meant. |
| 1293 | Tasks              | Feature     | **Choose how a task's priority appears on its card.** Asked for in GH #108, which proposed a coloured badge, a coloured border, or a small tag, and noted that you otherwise have to open a task to find out how urgent it is. A **live preview** sits under the options, built from the real card markup and the real stylesheet so it cannot drift from the board, and it previews **your own default priority rather than the word &ldquo;High&rdquo;** &mdash; a German install sees *Hoch* in the colour it has been given, which is the quickest possible confirmation of the fix in #1292. | 1292 | Tasks              | Fix         | **The priority dot was invisible on any install that renamed or translated its priorities.** Reported indirectly through GH #108, which asked for a priority indicator on task cards &mdash; there already is one, on by default, and the screenshot attached to the request did not show it. Every place that drew it built a CSS class out of the priority's **display name** (`priority-dot hoch`) and matched it against four hardcoded English rules &mdash; urgent, high, medium, low. Rename a priority, translate it, or simply add a fifth, and the class matched nothing: the element still rendered, as an eight-pixel **transparent** circle. No error, no fallback, no dot, and nothing on screen to suggest a setting had not been applied. This is the same disease as GH #79 and the Watchtower counters before it, and the cure is the same: the colour now comes from the colour picked against each priority in Settings, which is where an administrator already believed it came from. **It was four places, not one** &mdash; the board card, the list row, the subtask list inside a task, and the timeline &mdash; and the table view was already doing it correctly, which is the pattern the other four have been moved onto. Three further faults came out of it. **It was wrong in English too**: the seeded colours and the stylesheet had never agreed, so Low was configured green and drawn grey, and the swatch an administrator chose was not the colour they got. **The timeline defaulted an unrecognised name to `medium`**, so instead of showing nothing it showed a confident blue &mdash; a plausible wrong answer, which is worse than a blank. **And the priority name was written into an HTML attribute without being escaped**, so a name containing quotes could inject markup into every analyst's board; names are stored exactly as typed, and only the tooltip was ever escaped. All four now share one renderer with the colour validated as a literal hex value before it reaches the page and the name escaped on the way in. Also fixed while there: the list view called `.toLowerCase()` on the priority without checking there was one, and a task with no priority set would have thrown and taken the whole list render down with it. Proved in a browser across thirty cases &mdash; a German name, a name that never existed in English, a missing colour, a hostile colour, a hostile name, and the legacy on/off setting &mdash; and the checks were confirmed load-bearing by restoring the old behaviour and watching seven of them fail with `class="priority-dot hoch"` exactly as reported. |
| 1291 | Notifications      | Feature     | **Notifications can now be cleared, not just marked read.** Reported as GH #111: entries stayed in the bell for ever, long after the work behind them was finished. Worth being precise about what was actually wrong, because the button that looks like the answer is not one. **Mark all read only ever cleared the red badge.** It sets a read timestamp, and the list that draws the panel filters on whose notifications they are and nothing else &mdash; so every row stayed exactly where it was, losing a 3-pixel stripe down its left edge and nothing more. Press it and the panel looks unchanged, which reads as the button having failed. Nothing in the entire application had ever deleted a row from that table; there is no retention sweep and never was. The reason this survived unnoticed is worth recording too: on a development install **every notification was still unread**, so the state being complained about had never once been on screen. Each row now carries a **clear** button, and the panel header has **Clear all** beside Mark all read. Both ask before doing anything, since the delete is real and there is no undo &mdash; and the individual one matters more than it sounds, because that button sits a few pixels from the row it belongs to, so a mis-aimed tap would otherwise silently destroy the thing you were reaching for. **Clear all carries a safety catch**: on its own it removes only what you have already read, and a tick box &mdash; **off** every time it opens &mdash; extends it to the unread ones, saying how many that is. One click emptying the panel should not be able to bin news nobody has looked at yet. If everything is unread and the box is left alone it says so plainly rather than appearing to ignore the click. The rows are deleted outright rather than hidden: nothing else in the product reads that table, the durable record of what happened lives in the workflow events and each record's own history, so a dismissed row preserves nothing and needs no new column. Three things came out of building it. **The shared confirmation dialog gained an optional tick box**, which is the first time it has asked anything beyond yes or no &mdash; and it reports that answer through its callback rather than its return value, because **114 of its 129 call sites** do `if (await showConfirm(...))`, and handing them back an object instead of a boolean would make every Cancel in the product read as a confirm. **The clear button is drawn as a bordered circle rather than a bare cross that fades in on hover**: a mark that only appears once the pointer is already on it never announces that it can be clicked, and there is no hover at all on a phone, which would have left it permanently unreachable there. **And the "2 days ago" moved to the bottom row, hard right.** It used to sit beside the ticket reference, so against references of different lengths it landed somewhere different on every row; pinned to the right edge the ages line up into a column. Every path was driven in a real browser: clearing a row removes it without following the link it is sitting inside, cancelling keeps it, the keyboard reaches it, the badge and the chime's baseline both follow, and one analyst's ids match nothing against another's. English, German and Spanish. |

Worth recording *why* it survived: the page fits its screen perfectly, nothing overflows, and a test that scrolls the page from code succeeds even when a finger cannot &mdash; so every automatic check passed. **The From and To date filters on submissions were a mess**: their labels sat beside the fields and *&ldquo;From&rdquo;* is more than twice as wide as *&ldquo;To&rdquo;*, so two controls set by one rule started at different places and came out different lengths. It also says how many rules that show or hide *other* questions depend on the one you are removing and will go with it &mdash; which was happening silently before and is the part nobody could see coming. The headings are now **taken from the table's own heading row**, which is already on the page and already translated, so the card reads *&ldquo;Fields 7 &middot; Submissions 10&rdquo;* in whatever language the person is using, with no new wording invented and nothing to translate. | 1288 | Debug Tools        | Fix         | **D003 said an issuer mismatch "breaks login". It does not.** The check compares the issuer typed into the sign-in method against the one the provider's discovery document declares, and warned that a difference stops people signing in. It does not: the ID token's issuer is validated against the provider's own declared value, not against the field in FreeITSM, so the commonest cause of a mismatch &mdash; the `www` and bare forms of the same domain &mdash; signs in perfectly well. The line now shows what the provider calls itself, says plainly that sign-in still works, and notes that the two are usually meant to match. Found while working on #117, and worth correcting for exactly the reason that issue exists: a diagnostic that names the wrong culprit sends somebody hunting the wrong thing for a day. |
| 1287 | Debug Tools        | Improvement | **D003 now prints the address each OIDC endpoint actually points at, instead of just "present".** Reported as GH #117, where single sign-on redirected people to the FreeITSM host rather than the identity provider. The one fact that decides where a browser is sent &mdash; the `authorization_endpoint` the provider publishes &mdash; was the one fact the report did not state, and D003 could not have settled it either: it only said whether the endpoint existed. It now shows the value of `authorization_endpoint`, `token_endpoint` and `jwks_uri` (masked the same way the issuer already was, so Entra tenant IDs do not leak), says in one line what each is for, and raises two flags. **Not an absolute URL** is called out as the fault and named as an identity-provider misconfiguration, because that is the shape that masquerades as a bug in this application; it is also promoted into the verdict as a blocker. **A different host from the issuer** is a note rather than a failure, since Entra and Okta both legitimately do it &mdash; but when somebody is staring at an unexpected domain it is the line that explains why. The provider's `protocol` is now shown and schema-checked too, because the sign-in flow refuses anything that is not OIDC and a build missing that column would fail in a way this report could not previously explain. |
| 1286 | Authentication     | Fix         | **A misconfigured identity provider could send people to this server instead of to itself, and every symptom pointed at FreeITSM.** OpenID Connect is driven entirely by the provider's discovery document, and FreeITSM used its `authorization_endpoint` verbatim &mdash; correctly, since rewriting a provider's own address would be the real bug. But the spec requires that address to be absolute, and a misconfigured provider can publish a bare path such as `/oidc/authorize`. That was passed straight through into a `Location:` header, and a relative redirect is resolved **by the browser against the current origin** &mdash; so the user was sent to `https://your-freeitsm-host/oidc/authorize`, got a 404 from their own service desk, and nothing on screen implicated the provider. Discovery now refuses any of `authorization_endpoint`, `token_endpoint` or `jwks_uri` that is not an absolute `http(s)` URL, and the error names the identity provider as the thing to fix and shows the offending value. The check is deliberately stricter than PHP's own URL validator, which accepts `javascript:` and `data:` &mdash; schemes that must never reach a browser redirect. Reproduced end to end against a deliberately malformed discovery document before and after: without the guard the login endpoint really does emit `Location: /oidc/authorize?…`; with it, sign-in stops at the login page with a plain-English explanation. New `tests/oidc-discovery.php` (27 assertions) covers the relative and unsafe-scheme cases, the awkward-but-legal shapes real providers use, that discovery actually calls the guard, and &mdash; guarding against the regression the report alleged &mdash; that the authorization URL is still taken from the provider verbatim with no local host substituted. Same family as the relative-fetch fault in #74. |
| 1285 | Self-Service       | Improvement | **Tighter side margins when raising a ticket on a phone.** There were 47 pixels of framing down each edge before a field even began &mdash; the page's own margin, then the card's, then its border &mdash; which on a 360-pixel screen is a quarter of the width given over to empty space, leaving the subject box 266 pixels wide. It is now 25 pixels, and the fields are 310 wide. A detail worth recording for anyone wondering why the earlier attempt did nothing: the shared stylesheet already tried to narrow these margins on small screens, and had been losing silently to a more specific rule on this page for as long as both have existed. Unchanged on a computer, where the wider margins are right. |

| 1281 | Self-Service       | Fix         | **Opening one of your tickets on a phone no longer leaves you stuck.** The page could not be scrolled at all: the ticket, its history and the reply box ran well past the bottom of the screen with no way to reach them. The cause is a good example of two correct decisions being wrong together. On a computer the My Tickets screen deliberately pins the window in place so that the list and the ticket beside it each scroll independently, exactly as the analyst inbox does. On a narrow screen the two panes correctly stack into a single column instead &mdash; but nothing released the pinned window, so that column, now much taller than the screen, was simply cut off at the bottom with nothing able to scroll it. The page now scrolls normally on a phone, and does so as **one** movement rather than a list that scrolls inside a page that also scrolls, which is what makes a thumb swipe move the wrong thing. The e-mail verification page was measured at the same time and needed nothing. |
| 1279 | System             | Fix         | **Database Verification no longer reports a problem only a developer could fix.** After every update, the screen showed *&ldquo;The index list is out of date &mdash; run scripts/gen_db_verify_indexes.php and commit both files&rdquo;*, naming four database indexes, followed by the unrelated message *&ldquo;A valid table name is required&rdquo;*. Nothing was actually wrong with the installation, and there was nothing an administrator could usefully do about it. FreeITSM keeps a list of every database index so that it can restore one an older installation is missing, and that list is **generated** from the master schema file. Somebody added indexes to the schema without regenerating the list, so the two disagreed &mdash; and, because the check that spots this only runs when an administrator opens the Verification screen, the disagreement travelled out in a release and was reported by a user rather than caught here. The list is now regenerated and correct: it had been missing **sixteen** indexes, not the four that were visible. Two further changes so it does not recur. The generator can now be asked to **check** rather than write, naming exactly which indexes disagree and failing if they do, so a release can be stopped before it ships instead of the problem being discovered in somebody else's installation. And the second message is gone: the report includes a couple of rows that are notes rather than tables, and opening one asked the server to describe a table by that name, which it rightly refused &mdash; those rows now simply show their message. |

| 1263 | Tasks              | Feature     | **Tasks can now say when the work is happening, and record how long it took.** Requested by **mbsouth**, who wanted *&ldquo;multiple time periods with date, start and end times&rdquo;* against a task or subtask, and a total &mdash; because a task often cannot be finished in one sitting. An administrator chooses where this appears in **Tasks &rarr; Settings &rarr; Time**: on tasks, on subtasks, on both, or nowhere. Narrowing it **only hides**; nothing anybody recorded is deleted, and it reappears if the setting is widened again &mdash; and because a top-level task and a subtask are the same kind of record, a task dragged under a parent keeps its time either way. The setting governs saving as well as showing, so a page left open before it changed cannot quietly go on recording time against something an administrator has switched off. One subtlety worth knowing: the **planned** times are read exactly as typed by everybody, like a maintenance window &mdash; a 2pm slot is 2pm whoever is looking &mdash; while **recorded** time is a genuine moment and is shown in each reader's own timezone. |
| 1261 | Tasks              | Fix         | **A task edit that the server refused was thrown away without a word.** Found while fixing the sign-out problem above, and it is the reason that fault was so baffling to be on the receiving end of. When you change a field on a task, the browser sends it and &mdash; until now &mdash; **never looked at the answer**. A change the server accepted and a change it flatly refused produced exactly the same result on screen: nothing. So a refused edit did not fail, as far as anyone could tell; it simply did not happen, with the text you had typed already replaced by whatever the panel redrew. That is what made the sign-out fault present as *&ldquo;the page has frozen&rdquo;* rather than *&ldquo;you have been signed out&rdquo;*: the session had gone, every save was being turned away, and the board just sat there. The answer is now read, and a refusal is reported. **An expired session is called out by name**, because *&ldquo;failed to save&rdquo;* is no use when the real answer is *&ldquo;sign in again&rdquo;* &mdash; without that you retype the same sentence and watch it disappear repeatedly, which is precisely what was happening. Any other refusal shows the server's own reason rather than a generic apology, and a network drop is reported too. The same silence applied when **dragging a card to reorder it** in the list view: a refused move left the card springing back to where it started with nothing said, which reads as the drag not having worked rather than as the move being declined. |
| 1260 | System             | Fix         | **Being signed out in the middle of working, most often on the Tasks board.** Reported as *&ldquo;editing a task and saving forces a re-login&rdquo;*, and the Tasks board is where it shows up first, but the cause has nothing to do with tasks: FreeITSM was **letting PHP delete the sessions of people who were actively using it**. PHP decides a session is abandoned by looking at the timestamp on the session file, and deletes anything untouched for 24 minutes. That timestamp is normally kept fresh for you &mdash; PHP refreshes it whenever it closes a session at the end of a request, precisely so that somebody still working is never mistaken for somebody who has gone home. But **717 of FreeITSM's data endpoints deliberately close the session the instant they have read it**, which is what stops one slow request blocking every other request from the same browser, and that shortcut skips the refresh. Every one of those requests kept you signed in in every sense except the one being measured. The Tasks board is where it bites because it is a **single page**: you can work there for half an hour, and every edit is a background request, so nothing ever reloads the page and the clock never restarts. Move between tickets and each page load quietly resets it, which is why the same session survives there. Then any request at all has a one-in-a-hundred chance of running PHP's cleanup, which deletes the session of somebody who was mid-sentence, and the next click lands on the login screen. **Why it looked like a Docker problem**, and why it could not be reproduced on other installations: **nobody is immune, but the odds differ enormously.** The official Docker image ships PHP's own defaults, where the cleanup runs on one request in a hundred &mdash; often enough to catch somebody during an ordinary afternoon. A typical WAMP installation runs it on one request in a thousand, ten times rarer, and a developer reloading pages constantly restarts the clock long before it matters. Debian and Ubuntu switch the built-in cleanup off altogether and sweep from a scheduled job every half hour instead &mdash; which turns out to have the same blind spot, it simply gets far fewer chances to bite. Triggering it needs both halves at once: 24 minutes of work without a single page load, AND the cleanup happening to run in that window. Change either and it vanishes, which is why two people testing the same version in good faith could not reproduce it. FreeITSM now refreshes that timestamp itself on every request, restoring exactly what PHP would have done. Sessions that are genuinely idle still expire on exactly the same schedule as before, because the refresh only happens when a request is actually being served &mdash; which is the correct definition of *still in use*. |
| 1259 | Tasks              | Fix         | **Being given a task now tells you about it.** Assigning a task to somebody produced no notification at all &mdash; no badge on the bell, nothing in the list &mdash; so unless that person happened to open the Tasks board and look, they were never told there was work waiting for them. Tickets had always done this; tasks never had. The cause was not a broken notification but a **missing event**: FreeITSM announces things that happen to a task &mdash; created, completed, deleted &mdash; and *assigned* was simply not among them, so there was nothing for the bell to react to. Everything downstream was already built and waiting: the part that decides who to tell already knew that a task's recipient is its assignee, and the part that turns a notification into a link already knew how to open a task. Adding the event was most of the work. **It covers both ways a task is assigned.** Handing work out by creating a task with somebody's name already on it is the ordinary way it happens here, and a fix that only covered later reassignment would have missed the commoner case entirely. It is **on by default**, like its equivalent for tickets, and appears as its own switch under *Preferences &rarr; Notifications* for anyone who would rather it did not &mdash; including for people who had already saved notification settings before this existed, who get it switched on rather than silently missing. It is deliberately quiet in the cases where a notification would be noise: **you are never told about your own action**, so assigning something to yourself stays silent; saving a task again without changing who it belongs to does not tell them a second time; and removing an assignee is not an assignment, so nobody is told. The event is also now available to **workflows**, so it can trigger an email or anything else a workflow can do. |
| 1258 | System             | Fix         | **API keys could not be created, edited, switched off or deleted.** Every button on *System &rarr; API* answered with the same developer's error, *&ldquo;Unsupported Content-Type. Send application/json&rdquo;*, and nothing was saved. The screen had worked since it was built; what broke it was **FreeITSM's own security hardening**, added seven weeks later. That change refuses one particular kind of request &mdash; a specific trick used to forge requests across sites &mdash; and the API-keys screen, alone in the product, was making its four requests in exactly that shape. It was never a deliberate choice: a browser labels a request for you when you do not label it yourself, and the label it picks is precisely the one now refused. Three lines now say what they are sending, which is what the other 481 places in FreeITSM already did. **The more useful part of this fix is why nobody noticed for three weeks.** The security guard carried a written note claiming that every one of FreeITSM's 149 screens already labelled its requests correctly. That claim was untrue on the day it was written &mdash; these three had never done it &mdash; and being written down is exactly what stopped anyone checking, because a reader who wants to know reads the note instead of the code. The note has been replaced with a **test that checks it**: the security suite now reads every request in the entire codebase and fails if any of them would be turned away by our own defence. It proves itself in both directions before it is trusted &mdash; it is shown a faulty request and must object, and shown a correct one and must not &mdash; because a check that quietly matches nothing looks exactly like a clean pass. Reported by **jbournestreamsystems**, who diagnosed it correctly and supplied a patch for the three lines. |
| 1257 | Tickets            | Fix         | **Time logged from the right-click menu was recorded at the wrong time of day.** Reported on a system set to Vienna, where every entry made this way arrived **two hours later** than the time shown in the box that created it. Logging time from within the ticket itself was correct throughout, and the difference between the two is the whole explanation: the form inside the ticket sends no time at all and lets the server stamp it, while the right-click window offers you a date and time to adjust &mdash; and sent back exactly what was on screen, with nothing to say which part of the world it was written in. Every stored time in FreeITSM is held in **UTC** and converted for each person when it is displayed, so a bare *20:00* could only be taken as 20:00 UTC, and was then displayed to a Vienna reader as 22:00. There were in fact **two faults, one on each side of the same window**. The box also filled itself in from **the clock on your computer** rather than from the timezone you have chosen in FreeITSM &mdash; for somebody in London whose display timezone is set to Vienna, it opened offering 18:03 while every time on the screen behind it was written in Vienna time. That one produces no visible error when the two happen to agree, which is why it survived: it needs somebody whose machine and whose settings differ to see it at all. Both are corrected. The window now opens at the current time **in your own display timezone**, so it agrees with the list of entries directly beneath it, and the time you choose is converted before it is sent, so what you type is what you read back. The conversion is done in the one shared place FreeITSM keeps its date handling rather than in the ticket screen, since the same trap waits for any future screen that asks somebody to pick a date and time; it handles the hours either side of a daylight-saving change correctly, and falls back to the browser's own timezone for anybody who has not chosen one. **Existing entries are not altered** &mdash; there is no way to tell, after the event, which of them were typed in a different zone, and guessing would corrupt the ones that were right. |
| 1256 | System             | Feature     | **FreeITSM now warns you, before you update, if an update would destroy your files.** Reported by two Docker users whose attachments became unopenable after an update, with the message *&ldquo;That file is recorded but missing from storage.&rdquo;* Updating a Docker installation **replaces the container**, and anything inside it that has not been declared as a *volume* is discarded when that happens. The database is on a volume and survives, so what is left afterwards is a complete and correct set of records pointing at files that are gone &mdash; which reads as data corruption when in fact nothing in the application was at fault. **It cannot be undone**: the rebuild removes the old container and the files go with it, so there is nothing left to copy back. The only useful moment is therefore *before* the update, and that is now covered in three places. **The System screen** shows an unmissable notice naming every folder that would be lost and what is in each, so you meet the warning while you are already looking at the software rather than in documentation you would only read afterwards. **The setup screen** performs the same check on a brand-new installation &mdash; the most valuable place of the three, because at that point there is nothing to lose yet and correcting it costs nothing. On the setup screen it goes further than a red line in a list: because somebody who has just run one command cannot be expected to know what a Docker volume is, FreeITSM asks you to save a small **docker-compose.override.yml** rather than to edit `docker-compose.yml` &mdash; that file is part of the download, so editing it means a future update either loses your change or refuses to run at all, and the usual way out of a refused update silently discards it and puts you back where you started. Docker reads the override automatically. the exact lines to add are put on screen ready to copy, together with the order to do things in. The wording changes depending on whether anything is stored yet &mdash; an empty installation is simply told to add them, while one that already holds files is told to copy them out first, because adding a volume does not rescue what is already inside the container and following the wrong instruction is how somebody loses files while doing as they are told. And a new diagnostic, **D013 &mdash; Storage persistence**, lists every folder, says which would survive, and gives you the exact commands in the order they have to be run. All three share one implementation, so they cannot drift apart. The check is careful about what it claims: it says nothing at all on a WAMP, XAMPP or native Linux install, where the question does not apply, and it correctly recognises an installation that mounts the whole application folder as safe rather than raising a false alarm. Anything it cannot determine is reported as unknown rather than counted as a fault. The encryption key is singled out because losing it does not damage stored mailbox passwords and credentials, it makes them permanently unreadable. |

| 1254 | Knowledge          | Feature     | **The history of a document, or of a folder, can now be read.** FreeITSM has been recording who created, edited, read, moved and re-permissioned every article since folders were introduced &mdash; and there was no way to look at any of it, which made the audit trail a claim rather than a feature. | 1253 | System             | Fix         | **Copying a link or an API key silently failed on some phones.** Sharing a Knowledge article link on an iPhone copied nothing and said nothing at all. Ten of the twelve assumed it was always there, and the way that fails is unusually quiet &mdash; the error happens before the code that was meant to catch it and fall back, so the fallback never ran.
