| 1208 | System            | Feature     | **A new debug tool checks every attachment on a ticket, end to end.** **System &rarr; Debug Tools &rarr; D012** asks for a ticket reference and answers one question for every file on it: *would the download actually work, and if not, why?* It exists because **&ldquo;an attachment is broken&rdquo; is four different subsystems** &mdash; a file that arrived by email, a document attached to the ticket, a document attached to a note, and a screen recording. They share no table, no folder, no address and no numbering, so the first job is usually working out which one somebody means; the report names the subsystem and the exact link on every line, so a reporter's screenshot can be matched to a row without guessing. For each file it resolves the location **through FreeITSM's own code rather than a copy of the rule**, then checks the file is there, opens it, **reads every byte** &mdash; which is what catches a file that has been truncated or is locked by something else &mdash; compares its length and its fingerprint against what was recorded when it was uploaded, and finally **copies it out to a temporary folder, checks the copy matches, and deletes it again**, which is as close to a real download as can be done without a browser. Anything reported missing gets a second question asked of it: **is it genuinely gone, or is it there and unreachable?** The tool separates a file that has been deleted from one whose folder the server may not read, one excluded by a PHP security setting, and one **present under different capitalisation** &mdash; the last being what a move from a Windows server to a Linux one looks like, since Linux treats `Report.pdf` and `report.pdf` as two files and Windows does not. It also checks the **permission guards themselves**, calling the real ones and pairing every refusal with a case that should be allowed, because a guard that refuses everybody looks exactly like a guard that works. Where a check genuinely cannot run &mdash; there is no second company to be refused on a single-company installation &mdash; it says so rather than reporting a pass. |

The reason is that a date field is drawn by the phone itself, and **an iPhone ignores the width it is given** and sizes the field to the date it draws. It also spells the month out, showing `12 May 2026` where a desktop browser shows `12/05/2026`, so the field is considerably wider on a phone than on any computer. Zammad, which the suggestion came from, does this by painting internal notes red; FreeITSM does not, for two reasons. | 1200 | Search            | Fix         | **Searching for a value with a hyphen in it found nothing.** A customer number like `05145-8841815` sitting in an attached spreadsheet could not be found by typing it &mdash; while the same value typed with a space, `05145 8841815`, found it immediately. The cause: FreeITSM was **deleting** the punctuation from what you typed and gluing the rest together, so it went looking for `051458841815`. The search index had never seen that, because the indexer splits on punctuation exactly as you would expect and had stored `05145` and `8841815` as two separate words. The glued-up version existed nowhere, so the answer was a confident **no results**. The same fault hit ordinary words &mdash; `pre-flight` found nothing either. Punctuation inside a word is now treated as a space, exactly as if you had typed one, so `05145-8841815`, `05145.884`, `05145,884` and `05145 8841815` all behave identically and all find the file. Quoting a value &mdash; `"05145-8841815"` &mdash; still requires the parts to be adjacent, which is the way to be precise. **Two things this does not change**, both limits of the search engine rather than choices: a value typed with the punctuation *missing altogether* (`051458841815`) cannot match text that has it, and searching for the tail of a single word (`41815` inside `8841815`) will not match &mdash; searching for the start of one does, so `05145 884` finds it. |
| 1199 | Tasks             | Fix         | **Subtasks could not be ticked off.** Clicking a subtask's checkbox **opened the subtask instead of ticking it** &mdash; the click landed on the row underneath the box, and the row's job is to open things. Four separate faults were stacked on top of one another here, and each would have hidden the next. Underneath that, the code that marks a subtask complete asked the database for the status *literally named* &ldquo;Done&rdquo; &mdash; but those names are listed under **Tasks &rarr; Settings &rarr; Statuses** precisely so you can rename them, so on any installation that had (a German site calling it *Erledigt*, say) **a subtask could never be completed at all**. The tick itself was drawn by comparing the status to the English word &ldquo;Done&rdquo; too, so even a genuinely completed subtask showed an empty box. | 1196 | Self-Service Portal | Fix         | **The portal dashboard showed the wrong time.** The dashboard and the ticket list disagreed about the same ticket &mdash; and both were reading exactly the same field. FreeITSM stores every time in UTC, and the value arrives at the browser as a plain string that does not say so; the ticket list marked it as UTC, the dashboard did not, so the dashboard showed whatever the number happened to be in the reader's own timezone. That is **an hour early in British summer time, four hours late in New York, ten hours early in Sydney &mdash; and exactly right all winter in the UK**, which is why it went unnoticed: a wrong time is still a real, plausible, correctly-formatted time, and for five months of the year it was not even wrong. The cause was not the one missing marker. The self-service portal had **no shared date handling at all** &mdash; no timezone, no common helpers &mdash; so each of its pages had written its own, and two of the three happened to get it right. The portal now uses the same date handling as the rest of FreeITSM, wired in one shared place, so all its pages agree by construction. A related oddity went with it: the ticket list decided whether to show a time or a date by asking whether the ticket fell on *today* in the browser's timezone rather than the one the time was being displayed in, which is how an entry ends up labelled with one day beside a time from another. |

Proven by running the same 24 checks against the old and the new code and confirming the output is identical, then exercising the real save endpoint over HTTP &mdash; the estate came out byte for byte as it went in. | 1129 | Tickets           | Improvement | **Help and documentation for everything above.** In the application, **Tickets &rarr; Help &rarr; Settings** gains a prominent **Automatic emails &amp; signatures** guide, in the same style as the SLA and Mailbox Authentication ones: merge codes and `[ticket_url]`, the public web address every emailed link depends on and why a scheduled send cannot work it out for itself, limiting a template to particular senders and why the order they are listed in deliberately does not matter, checking what a given sender would actually get, what a **Not sent** row in the outbound log means, and how signatures work for the analysts who write them. It ends with a symptom-to-cause table &mdash; including the two that look like faults and are not: only one template is ever sent per event, and a reply signed with the wrong person's name means a signature using `[analyst_name]` (the ticket's owner) rather than `[my_name]` (whoever is typing). On the wiki, two new developer guides for the sender rules and for signatures, and five pages updated because this work made them **wrong rather than merely incomplete**: the send log had two possible results and now has three, the canned-response and Tickets pages listed the merge codes without `[ticket_url]`, and both issue-tracker developer guides described a link builder that has since moved and had a subfolder fault fixed in it. |
| 1128 | Tickets           | Feature     | **Your signature now goes into replies.** The other half of [#1127](https://github.com/edmozley/freeitsm/discussions/80): open a reply or a forward and your default signature is already there, with a blank line above it to write in. **It is put into the editor, not added when you press Send** &mdash; so you can read it, change it, or delete it for this one email, and what you see in front of you is what the customer receives. A signature stapled on invisibly at send time is how somebody ends up with two sign-offs, or the wrong one, and never finds out. A **Signature** button sits beside Templates above the message box: it lists everything you have, marks which is the default, swaps the one in the draft for another, or takes it out altogether. If you have not written a signature yet the menu says so and links straight to where you write one. Nothing is inserted if the list could not be loaded, rather than a reply going out with a signature nobody chose. One small thing that had to be got right: an empty editor reports itself as having no content at all, so the blank paragraph to type in is put there deliberately &mdash; without it the signature becomes the first thing in the message and the cursor lands in the middle of your own sign-off. |
| 1127 | System            | Feature     | **Analysts can now keep their own email signatures.** The third request in [discussion #80](https://github.com/edmozley/freeitsm/discussions/80), and the groundwork for the rest of it. Under **Preferences** (your name &rarr; Preferences) there is now **Email signatures**, where you write a signature with the usual formatting &mdash; bold, lists, a link &mdash; and drop in merge codes for your own details. **Signatures are per analyst and nothing else**: there is deliberately no shared or install-wide signature to administer, because a signature is a person signing their own name, and one signature for a whole team is either wrong for everybody or has to be filled in by merge codes anyway. Nobody else can see or change yours &mdash; every request is scoped to whoever is signed in rather than to an id that could be pointed at somebody else. **You may keep more than one** &mdash; a formal one for customers and a short one for colleagues, or one per language if you answer in more than one &mdash; and exactly one is the **Default**. That matters more than it sounds: the default is the one added automatically, so an analyst who only ever wants a single signature never sees a choice at all, and picking a different one stays a deliberate act rather than a decision taxed on every reply. Your first signature becomes the default whether or not you ask for it, since a signature nothing ever uses reads as the feature simply not working. **A new My details section** holds job title, department, phone and mobile, which are new to an analyst record &mdash; they had only a name and an email address, so a "template driven" signature would have had almost nothing to merge. The editor previews as you type, filling the codes in from your own details including ones you have typed but not yet saved, and **a code you have no value for is removed rather than left showing** &mdash; nobody wants `[my_mobile]` at the bottom of every email they send. Worth knowing: `[analyst_name]`, which the ticket templates use, means the ticket's owner and **not** the person typing, so signatures use their own `[my_name]` and friends. Signing Sam's reply with Jo's name because Jo happens to own the ticket is exactly the sort of thing nobody notices until a customer does. **Nothing inserts a signature into a reply yet** &mdash; that is the next step. |
| 1126 | Tickets           | Feature     | **Automatic replies can now be limited to particular senders.** The second request in [discussion #80](https://github.com/edmozley/freeitsm/discussions/80): the auto-reply fired for every ticket created from email regardless of who sent it, so external senders received an internal-sounding response. Any email template can now be scoped to an email address, a whole domain, or several of either &mdash; and a template with nothing set applies to everyone, which is how every new template starts. **The part that took the thinking is what decides which template wins.** The obvious approach &mdash; work down the list, use the first one that matches &mdash; means an administrator has to get the rules right *and* the ordering right, with nothing to tell them when the second is wrong. Instead **the most specific template wins**: one naming an exact address beats one naming that address's domain, and both beat one that goes to everyone. Dragging rows up and down cannot change what is sent, so there is no ordering to get wrong. Worth knowing if you have ever wondered why a second template did nothing: **until now exactly one template per event was ever used &mdash; the one that happened to sort first &mdash; and any others were silently ignored.** Two things guard the gap this opens up. **Check what a sender would get** on the Email Templates screen takes an address and names the template that would go back and why, using the same code that chooses it for real rather than a second copy that could disagree. And where every template for an event has been restricted, the screen says plainly that a sender matching none of them will get nothing. **Neither of those helps twelve months later**, when a new customer domain is onboarded by people who never saw that screen &mdash; so an email that is not sent because nobody matched is now recorded against the ticket and in the mailbox's outbound log as **Not sent**, with the reason. That log had two possible outcomes before, sent and failed, and a deliberate non-send would have been shown as *Sent*, which is the one answer worse than no answer at all. |
| 1125 | Tickets           | Feature     | **Email templates can now link straight back to the ticket, and the body has formatting controls.** From [discussion #80](https://github.com/edmozley/freeitsm/discussions/80). A new merge code **`[ticket_url]`** resolves to the requester's own view of their ticket in the self-service portal, so a *"we've logged your request"* email can carry a **track it here** link rather than leaving somebody to go and find the ticket themselves. It is offered in canned responses too, since both kinds of template have always drawn from the same list. The template body was a plain box in which any formatting had to be typed as HTML by hand; it now has a small toolbar &mdash; bold, italic, underline, lists, links &mdash; kept deliberately short, because the formatting that survives a mail client is a short list. The **&lt;&gt;** button is still there for anyone who wants to write the markup themselves, and the **Preview** tab still shows the email with every merge code filled in. **The part worth knowing about is the address.** These emails are usually sent by the mail collector on a schedule, and at that moment nobody is using FreeITSM &mdash; there is no browser request to work out the site's address from, so a link built at 3am would have no site name in it and would not work. The Email Templates screen therefore now carries the **public web address** this installation answers on, and if a template uses `[ticket_url]` while nothing is set it says so, once, in a message that can be dismissed if it does not apply to you. **This also fixed a link that has always been slightly wrong**: the same address is used for links FreeITSM puts into Jira and Azure DevOps work items, and an installation served from a folder rather than a whole domain lost that folder from the address, so the developer clicking through landed on a page that was not there. |
| 1124 | System            | Fix         | **Nobody could change the default password on a brand-new installation.** Reported in [issue #74](https://github.com/edmozley/freeitsm/issues/74). On first sign-in FreeITSM insists you replace the seeded password before it will let you do anything else, and the page it sends you to asked the server for `api/myaccount/change_password.php` **without saying where FreeITSM is installed**. That address only resolves when the page is reached at one of the two web addresses it answers on &mdash; and [the fix to issue #68](https://github.com/edmozley/freeitsm/issues/68) had just changed the application to send people to the other one. The result was a form that looked perfectly normal, a button that did nothing at all, and a browser console filling with *404*. Because it only appears on a first sign-in, **the one install this stops dead is the one nobody has used yet.** It was four pages rather than one, all with the same fault: the same page asked for the same address the same way, **the one-time-code step of sign-in** did it too &mdash; so on any installation with two-factor authentication switched on, nobody could finish signing in either &mdash; and so did **Forgot password** and **Reset password**. Two of those four turned out never to have loaded FreeITSM's configuration at all, so they had no way of knowing where the application lived even to ask: their *"you are already signed in"* redirect has been sending people to the wrong place on every installation served from a subfolder. All four now build their addresses from the application root, which is worked out from where the files sit on disk rather than from the address the visitor happened to arrive on, so each page behaves identically at both of its addresses. |
| 1123 | System            | Improvement | **Help and documentation for everything above.** In the application, **Tickets &rarr; Help &rarr; Mailbox authentication** gains a section on the **Default ticket origin** and on the **!** beside a mailbox name &mdash; what it flags, why warnings can be dismissed while errors cannot, and what is deliberately not flagged at all. **Watchtower &rarr; Help** gains a section on its new settings screen, including the two judgements FreeITSM cannot make for you: which morning-check statuses count as a problem, and which service problems turn the light red. | 1122 | Watchtower        | Fix         | **The browser extension's badge ignored failed morning checks, and undercounted open tickets.** The toolbar badge and its popup read the same dashboard data as Watchtower itself, and carried the same faults: they counted a morning-check status called **Fail**, which FreeITSM has never had &mdash; the statuses it ships are Green, Amber and Red &mdash; so a morning where every check failed added **nothing** to the badge and never turned it red. The popup's ticket figure added up the three statuses called Open, In Progress and On Hold, so tickets in any other open status were missing from it, and its task figure did the same with To Do and In Progress. All of them now read the same figures the dashboard does. **Which morning-check statuses count as needing attention is now worked out in one place on the server** and shared by the dashboard, the badge and the popup, rather than each deciding for itself &mdash; which is how all three came to be counting a status that did not exist. The popup also says *"all completed"* rather than *"all passed"*, since nothing records which of your statuses is a pass, and it now names your busiest open ticket status rather than assuming one is called *In Progress*. |
| 1121 | Watchtower        | Improvement | **The Watchtower settings screen now says which module each row belongs to, and colours it accordingly.** Every setting on that page changes how some *other* module is reported, which is easy to lose track of when the whole lot is listed together &mdash; *"Impact levels that turn the light red"* does not announce that it is about Service Status. | 1120 | Watchtower        | Improvement | **Service Status joins the settings screen: which impact levels appear, and which turn the light red.** Two entries under **Watchtower &rarr; Settings &rarr; Counts**. The first decides what puts a service on the card &mdash; left alone, anything other than your healthy level does, so untick planned maintenance if you would rather it stayed off an attention board without pretending it is not happening. The second decides which levels are serious enough for a red light, with everything else amber. **The second one exists to undo a knot rather than to add a knob.** Red previously followed each level's *counts as downtime* setting, which sounds reasonable until you want a degraded service drawn amber: that setting decides whether time at the level counts against your **uptime percentages**, so the only way to change the colour was to falsify your uptime reporting. They are now separate questions with separate answers, and leaving the new one alone keeps today's behaviour exactly. |
| 1119 | Watchtower        | Fix         | **A total outage was drawn amber, in the mildest style, if you had renamed the impact level.** The Service Status card decided whether to show red or amber by comparing the level's name against the words *Major Outage* and *Partial Outage*, and picked one of four badge styles by matching *Major Outage*, *Partial Outage* and *Maintenance*. Those are the very levels that were made renameable when the status board was fixed &mdash; so on an installation that had renamed or translated them, the single most serious thing the dashboard can report was downgraded to amber and given the gentlest-looking badge. **A level you added yourself never matched any of them**, so a custom *Degraded Performance* &mdash; which counts against your uptime &mdash; could never turn the light red either. Red now follows the level's own **counts as downtime** setting, which is exactly the question being asked, and each badge is drawn in **the colour you gave that level**, so a renamed, translated or newly invented level appears correctly without being listed anywhere in the code. One consequence worth knowing: *Degraded* counts as downtime by default, so a degraded service now shows red rather than amber &mdash; if that is not how your team reads it, turn off "counts as downtime" on that level and the light follows. Service and impact names were also being written into the page without escaping, and now are. |
| 1118 | Watchtower        | Improvement | **The Changes card was showing two figures that looked like they contradicted each other.** *"2 In Progress"* sat inches from *"1 change in progress now"* &mdash; two different questions wearing the same name. The first counts where changes are **sitting**; the second counts what is **happening this minute**, worked out from the scheduled work window. The second line is now worded *"inside their work window now"*, so the two stop colliding. **The gap between them turned out to be the most useful thing on the card, and nothing was showing it**: a change whose scheduled window finished but which nobody ever moved on. It counted towards the status figure and was excluded from the work-window figure, so it fell between the two and appeared in neither &mdash; on a dashboard whose whole job is to surface what needs attention, the overrunning change is close to the point. It now has its own line: **"N changes past their scheduled window and still open"**. |
| 1117 | Watchtower        | Improvement | **The Changes card now shows changes by status, like Tickets and Tasks do &mdash; and you can choose which statuses appear.** It was the odd one out: its three figures are worked out from dates and approvals rather than from statuses, so the card could tell you what was scheduled, active or awaiting a decision but could never answer *"how many changes are sitting at Submitted?"* &mdash; the one thing the other two cards answer at a glance. It now leads with a total and one figure per open status, under the name and colour you gave it, with **Change statuses shown** added to **Watchtower &rarr; Settings &rarr; Counts** alongside the others. The three original lines keep their place underneath, unchanged and unaffected by the choice: they are derived from work dates and approvals, so *"2 In Progress"* and *"1 change in progress now"* can legitimately differ &mdash; one is where changes are sitting, the other is what is actually happening at this minute. | 1116 | Watchtower        | Fix         | **Unsubmitted draft changes were being counted as awaiting approval.** Reading "awaiting approval" from whether the change has actually been approved &mdash; rather than from what its status happens to be called &mdash; was right, but it was too broad: a **Draft** has not been approved either, and it appeared on the count as though somebody owed it a decision. A draft is nobody's turn. The count now also requires that the change has moved off the status it started in, which is the fact that distinguishes "submitted and waiting on you" from "still being written" without naming a single status. The same rule is applied to *scheduled* and *in progress now*, because a change nobody has submitted is not scheduled and is not being worked on, whatever dates have been pencilled into it. | 1115 | Watchtower        | Fix         | **The Counts tab on the new Watchtower settings screen did nothing when clicked.** The tab bar is drawn by shared code that calls a switching function each settings page supplies, and this page &mdash; being the first new settings screen in a while &mdash; never supplied one. Both tabs were fully built and loaded; only the click had nowhere to go. |
| 1114 | Watchtower        | Feature     | **Watchtower has a settings screen.** It never had one, which was odd for the busiest screen in FreeITSM &mdash; and it did already have settings, they just had nowhere to live: the *"paused too long"* threshold has been read on every dashboard load since it was added and could only ever be changed by editing the database by hand. It now has a box. **Cards** turns any of the ten cards off for installations that don't watch them &mdash; nothing is lost, and each module still shows everything in its own screens. **Counts** decides what each figure is counting. By default every count includes **every status you have**, which is what makes a renamed or newly added status work without being mentioned anywhere in here; narrow one only when a card is showing more than you want to read at a glance. The screen only ever *trims* a dashboard that is already correct &mdash; leave it alone and nothing changes &mdash; which is deliberate, because if ticking boxes were what made the numbers right, every installation would be wrong until somebody found this page, and a blank dashboard reads as *"nothing needs attention"*. **The "high priority tickets" line now names the priorities it counted** &mdash; *(High, Critical, Urgent)* &mdash; rather than describing itself as "urgent/high" for ever regardless of what was chosen or what your priorities are called. And **the one judgement FreeITSM genuinely could not make for you now has a home**: nothing anywhere records which of your morning-check statuses is a pass and which is a problem, so until you say, the card assumes only the first status in your own order is good and never claims checks have *passed*, only that they are *done*. Tell it which statuses need attention and it will use that instead. The settings themselves are stored against the dashboard rather than as flags on your statuses, because *"show this on my dashboard"* is a fact about the dashboard &mdash; your statuses carry their own facts, which the SLA clock and much else depend on, and one screen's preferences have no business mixed in with them. Two separate permissions, because hiding a card tidies a screen while changing what a count includes changes what a number **means**. |
| 1113 | Watchtower        | Fix         | **Watchtower was counting by typed-in words, and several of them were wrong.** Fourteen places asked the database for statuses and priorities *by name* &mdash; `'Open'`, `'In Progress'`, `'To Do'`, `'Urgent'`, `'Fail'` &mdash; and a name that matches nothing quietly counts nothing, so every one of them failed as a confident zero rather than as an error. Three were already wrong in English, on a stock installation, with nothing renamed: **The open-ticket headline was undercounting.** It added up the three statuses called Open, In Progress and On Hold, so a ticket sitting in **Awaiting Response** &mdash; a status FreeITSM ships as standard &mdash; was missing from the number altogether. On the developer's own system it read 88 against a true figure of 100. **Morning Checks could report a clean sweep on a morning when every check was red.** The card counted statuses named `OK`, `Warning` and `Fail`; the statuses FreeITSM actually ships are **Green, Amber and Red**, so all three counts sat at nought for ever, the "checks failed" alert could never appear, and the green *"all checks completed and passing"* line &mdash; which was conditioned on those same empty counts &mdash; appeared regardless of the results underneath it. **Completed and failed changes were being counted as upcoming work**, because the filter excluded two status names (`Closed`, `Cancelled`) and FreeITSM has never had a change status called Closed &mdash; of the four finished statuses it caught one. Every one of these now reads a fact instead of a word. Cards list **one entry per status that genuinely exists**, under the name and in the colour you gave it, so a status you add appears by itself and a status you rename keeps working &mdash; in your language, without a translation. *Changes awaiting approval* is read from whether the change has actually been approved rather than from what its status is called, so an extra approval stage doesn't need adding to a list in the code. *Changes in progress* uses the work window, which already says precisely that. **High-priority tickets** now means *ranked above your default priority* &mdash; on stock data exactly the same three as before, and the same number, but a priority you add above Normal is now counted rather than silently left out of the very tile meant to catch it. Morning Checks shows a green light only when every check sits in the **most favourable status you have defined**, and says *"all checks completed"* rather than *"passing"*, because nothing in FreeITSM records which of your statuses is a pass. Found while fixing [#79](https://github.com/edmozley/freeitsm/issues/79). |
| 1112 | Tickets           | Feature     | **Each mailbox now says where its tickets came from &mdash; and flags anything quietly wrong with itself.** Tickets arriving by email were not marked as having come from email at all, so the **Source** field sat empty and no report could tell email tickets from any other kind. Rather than stamping every mailbox with the word *Email*, each mailbox carries its own **Default ticket origin**, chosen from a dropdown in its settings. That is the more useful answer as well as the safer one: a helpdesk address and a monitoring address both arrive as email, and marking an automated alert from your monitoring platform as though somebody had written in is only accurate in the narrowest sense. Point one mailbox at *Email* and another at an origin you have added called *Monitoring*, and the tickets can finally be told apart. **The origin is stored as a reference rather than as the word itself**, so renaming it later changes what you see everywhere and breaks nothing &mdash; the failure that caused the bug above. On installations with more than one company, a mailbox pinned to a company may use that company's own origins as well as the standard ones, while a shared mailbox may use only the standard ones, because its tickets land in whichever company the sender's domain matches and one client's private label has no business on another client's ticket. The standard origins are always available, so there is no mailbox that cannot be given one. **Every mailbox also gains an ! beside its name.** Clicking it lists everything that could be wrong with that mailbox in plain terms, each item saying what the consequence is rather than just naming a setting: no ticket origin, **reading the wrong inbox**, never signed in, switched off, not checked for mail in days, set to file imported mail into a folder that was never named, or an IMAP mailbox with no outgoing server so replies cannot be sent. This exists because of how the original fault was found &mdash; the mailbox was authenticated, green, and collecting mail perfectly, and the only sign anything was wrong turned up weeks later on the tickets themselves. A mailbox with nothing wrong has no mark at all. **Any warning can be dismissed**, because most of them describe something you may well have meant: a mailbox that genuinely should record no origin, or a receive-only address with no outgoing server. Dismissing says *"I know"* &mdash; the mark clears, and the item stays listed inside, with a **Restore** next to it, so acknowledging something is not the same as hiding it. That matters more than it sounds: a warning sign that can never be cleared is one people stop reading, and it would have taken the useful marks down with it. **Errors cannot be dismissed** &mdash; reading the wrong inbox is a fault rather than a preference, and this is the one place where letting somebody silence it would be worse than never having said anything. Two things are deliberately not flagged at all, being ordinary choices already shown as a badge on the row: a mailbox switched off, and a mailbox left as shared intake rather than pinned to a company. Asked for in [#79](https://github.com/edmozley/freeitsm/issues/79) by tjedelhauser. |
| 1111 | Tickets           | Fix         | **A new ticket arrived with no status at all if you had renamed the "Open" status.** The status column in the ticket list was blank, the **Status** dropdown opened with nothing chosen, and changing the status to anything else and back put it right permanently &mdash; which is the signature of a value that was never set rather than one that was set wrongly. Every route that opens a ticket &mdash; mail, the self-service portal, web chat and the other messaging channels, the service catalogue, and the workflow engine &mdash; asked the database for the status **named "Open"**. That is a display name you are invited to edit under Tickets &rarr; Settings, so on an installation where it had been renamed or translated &mdash; *Offen*, on the German site where this was reported &mdash; the question had no answer and the ticket was filed with **no status**, silently, because a ticket is permitted to have none. Which status a new ticket starts in is now read from the one you have **marked as the default**, so it survives any rename, and it falls back sensibly if that status has since been switched off. **Priority was asked for by name in exactly the same breath and mostly got away with it**, because *Normal* happens to be the same word in German; it is now read from the default too, rather than waiting for the first installation to rename it. **The ticket header was quietly making this harder to spot:** with no status stored it displayed *"Open"* anyway &mdash; a placeholder, not the truth &mdash; so the header and the list disagreed about the same ticket and neither was obviously wrong. It now says **None**, which is what is actually true. The same header also reverted **Department** and **Owner** to English *None* and *Unassigned* the moment any property was changed, on a site running in another language. **Tickets already created this way are repaired by System &rarr; Database Verify**, which now gives any ticket missing a status or priority the default one. That repair existed but could never run where it was needed: it sat behind a check for a database column that only installations upgraded from a much older version still have, so a fresh installation &mdash; the only kind that could hit this &mdash; skipped it. Reported as [#79](https://github.com/edmozley/freeitsm/issues/79) by tjedelhauser, whose report also covered the empty **Source** field &mdash; that half is the entry above. |
| 1110 | Tickets           | Feature     | **Time recording can be switched off.** Plenty of internal IT teams care about resolving the ticket and writing it up, not about how many minutes it took &mdash; and until now the time panel sat there regardless. **Tickets &rarr; Settings &rarr; Time tracking** turns it off, and the panel disappears from the ticket view. **Nothing is deleted:** anything already recorded stays exactly where it is and comes back untouched the moment you turn it on again. There are **two switches, not one**, and the second is the important one: hiding the panel tidies your screens, but closing the REST API can break an integration somebody built against it &mdash; a billing export, a reporting job &mdash; so they are separate decisions and you can make them separately. **Both can be set per company**, with an install-wide default each company follows unless told otherwise; which switch applies to a ticket is decided by the company that ticket belongs to, so an MSP can bill one client for time and not another. On a single-company installation there is no company column at all &mdash; just the two switches. Suggested in [discussion #72](https://github.com/edmozley/freeitsm/discussions/72) by dschipfel. |
| 1109 | System            | Improvement | **Documents can be found by what is inside them, not only what they are called.** The text of an attached PDF, Word file or spreadsheet is read in the background and added to the search index, so &#8984;K finds the contract that *mentions* a clause rather than only the one named after it &mdash; under a **Found inside documents** heading, next to the existing "found inside tickets". Reading PDFs and scans needs [Apache Tika](https://tika.apache.org/) configured under System &rarr; Search; without it a document is still findable by its name and description, and the ⓘ says which. A file waiting to be read says **"Not searchable yet"** rather than nothing, because "we have not read it" and "there is nothing in it to read" are different facts that otherwise look identical. |
| 1108 | System            | Feature     | **Attach documents to anything.** Contracts, assets, knowledge articles, problems and changes can all carry documents &mdash; drag a file in, or paste a link to one held in SharePoint, Google Drive or whatever document system you already use. **A link is a first-class document**, so there is no pressure to move anything: FreeITSM either holds the file or points at it, and the list looks the same either way. **The same document can be attached to several records** &mdash; one warranty covering eleven laptops is stored once, not eleven times &mdash; and an ⓘ on every document shows everywhere it lives, so you can see that removing it from here may not remove it everywhere. **Who can see a document is decided entirely by what it is attached to:** if you can see the contract you can read its documents, and if you cannot, the document does not appear in the list, in search, in &#8984;K, or at its own web address. Nothing needs configuring for that &mdash; it follows the access you already have, and it keeps following it when access changes. Detaching a document leaves it alone if it is still attached elsewhere, and only deletes it when the last record lets go. Asked for in [discussion #76](https://github.com/edmozley/freeitsm/discussions/76) by dschipfel. |
| 1107 | Tickets           | Fix         | **Collecting mail from any folder other than Inbox failed on Microsoft 365.** Setting **Email folder** to your own folder &mdash; `freeitsm`, say &mdash; produced *"Failed to fetch emails. HTTP 400. ErrorInvalidIdMalformed"* and nothing was ever collected. Microsoft's API does not accept folder **names** in that position: it takes a small fixed list of built-in names (Inbox, Archive, Sent Items and a few more) and treats anything else as an internal folder identifier, which a name is not. So `INBOX` had only ever worked because it is on that list &mdash; reading a folder **by name had never worked at all**, for any name off it. The name is now looked up properly and turned into the identifier before use. **Folders inside other folders now work too**, written with a slash (`Inbox/freeitsm`), because putting the intake folder under Inbox is the first thing most people try and it would otherwise report "not found" for a folder plainly visible in Outlook. **The Email folder box also gains a Verify button.** It was the one folder field that never had one: the *move imported mail to* box below it could confirm `Folder "freeitsm" found (1 items, 1 unread)` while the box above it &mdash; the one that decides where mail is read from &mdash; silently could not use the same folder. Both boxes now check through the same code, so they cannot disagree again. Reported as [#77](https://github.com/edmozley/freeitsm/issues/77) by tjedelhauser. |
| 1106 | Notifications     | Fix         | **The notification bell opened to nothing on the home page.** The red count was right &mdash; it said 3 &mdash; and clicking it gave you an empty panel. The bell is drawn from the shared header, so it appears on every page, but the home page was the one page that never loaded the translation script the rest of the application does. The very first thing the bell does when opened is ask for the word *"Loading&hellip;"*, and with nothing to ask, it stopped there: **the request for your notifications was never sent at all**, and the error handler that would have said "couldn't load" sat one line further down than the failure, so it never ran either. Nothing appeared in the log and the badge went on counting correctly, which is why it read as *"you have no notifications"* rather than as a fault. **Two other pages had exactly the same hole and are fixed too &mdash; System, and Problem Management** &mdash; found by checking every page in the application rather than only the one that was reported. Reported as [#78](https://github.com/edmozley/freeitsm/issues/78) by tjedelhauser. Loading the translations on the home page also puts it in line for being translated, which it never has been on the browser side. |
| 1105 | System            | Feature     | **Two new checks, under System &rarr; Debug Tools.** **D010 &mdash; Sign-in methods, and how you are signed in** lists every sign-in method and its state, says what the login page will actually offer a visitor, and &mdash; the part that is hard to get any other way &mdash; names the route *you personally* used to get in. An administrator looking at the Authentication screen has by definition already signed in, so "nobody can get in" and "everything is fine" look identical from that chair. It reads the two master switches **as stored** rather than as drawn, and if the answer is that nothing at all is on offer it says so and names the `?local=1` break-glass. **D011 &mdash; Directory sync readiness** asks a different question of the same rows: not *can anybody sign in with this* but *could this import people*. It audits every table and column directory sync needs against the database's own canonical definition &mdash; so it cannot drift as the feature grows &mdash; distinguishes a column that is **missing** from one that is **empty** from one that is **NULL**, since those are three different faults with three different fixes, and then walks each method through the gates in the order the code applies them and names **the one blocker** rather than listing everything unset. It also dumps the stored value that decides whether a row offers **Configure** or **Edit**, byte for byte with its length, because `LDAP` and `ldap ` both quietly render a directory as though it were an OIDC provider. **Both reports are built to be sent to somebody**: usernames, email local-parts, bind accounts and every value inside a DN are masked, while attribute names and the shape of the directory tree &mdash; the half that is actually diagnostic &mdash; are kept. |
| 1104 | System            | Fix         | **The Authentication screen could show you two switches that had never loaded.** *Enable single sign-on* and *Allow local login* are drawn unticked and then filled in from the server, so a failed load looked exactly like **both switches off** &mdash; which is to say, like an installation nobody can sign into. The page said nothing; the failure went to the browser console. Worse, **Save** would then have written that guess back as fact, turning off single sign-on and the password form together in one click, from a screen that never claimed to have read anything. A failure now says so plainly, the switches and Save are locked until the real values arrive, and a **Retry** puts it right without reloading. The code already treated an absent *Allow local login* as **on**, because on is the safe answer; the blank checkbox said the opposite. |
| 1103 | Service Status    | Fix         | **Renaming the "Operational" impact level broke the status board.** A service with an open incident showed the new name; every service without one carried on saying *Operational* and lost the colour from its badge &mdash; so the same level appeared twice, under two names, one of them grey. The cause is that a healthy service has no impact level stored anywhere: with no incident there is nothing to record, so the status is worked out on the fly, and six separate places in the code worked it out by writing the word *Operational* into the answer. Which level means "nothing is wrong" is now read from the level you have marked as the default, and its colour is sent with it, so a level that has been renamed **or** switched off still paints its badge. This ran deeper than the board: the portal's **All systems operational** banner tested for that same literal word, so once the level was renamed it could never appear again; Watchtower's list of affected services excluded the level by name, so a rename would have filled it with every healthy service you own; and creating an incident through the API without naming an impact failed outright with *"Unknown or inactive impact level"*. A custom level added alongside the stock ones &mdash; *Degraded Performance*, say &mdash; was also shown in the portal in Operational green, because it matched nothing in a hardcoded list of five names. |
| 1102 | System            | Improvement | **The directory screens are now translated into German, Norwegian (Bokmål and Nynorsk) and Brazilian Portuguese.** Every string on the Authentication provider screens &mdash; connection, sign-in, importing, field mapping and history &mdash; not just the new ones. Malay and Ukrainian are still to come; the remaining 17 languages do not carry the System module at all yet, which is a wider gap than this feature. |
| 1101 | System            | Improvement | **An import now notices when part of your directory has been renamed.** What you tick is stored as a location in the directory, and locations change when somebody reorganises an OU. Both ways of failing were silent. **A branch you selected that no longer exists now stops the import outright, changes nothing, and names the branch** &mdash; importing the branches that do still exist is exactly how everybody in the missing one ends up marked as having left. **A branch you deliberately excluded that no longer exists lets the import run, but says so loudly**, because the people you left out have started arriving &mdash; and nothing else would ever have told you: the safety brake only watches for a sudden *drop*, so people being added is invisible to it. Installations that type a starting point by hand are unaffected and are never warned. |
| 1100 | System            | Feature     | **Pick what to import by ticking it, instead of typing a distinguished name.** **Browse directory** on the Importing people tab draws your directory as a tree and puts a head count beside every branch, so you can see that ticking *Staff* brings in 32 people **before** you run anything &mdash; rather than typing `OU=Staff,OU=Company,DC=…` and finding out afterwards. **Ticking a branch means the whole branch, including anything added to it later**, so a department created next year imports on its own without anybody remembering to come back here. To leave one part out &mdash; contractors, service accounts, a site that belongs to somebody else &mdash; untick it inside the ticked branch and it is struck through and skipped. What is stored is the exceptions, not a list of members: a list would freeze your selection at today's shape of the directory and nothing would tell you when it went stale. Installations that already import carry on **exactly** as before, since a typed starting point is still honoured when nothing is ticked, and the box is still there for a directory the service account cannot browse &mdash; clearly marked when the tree overrides it. |
| 1099 | System            | Fix         | **The import history was squeezed into half the screen.** On a wide monitor the page arranges its settings in two columns, and the history table was being arranged along with them &mdash; so a nine-column table sat in half a screen with its heading wrapped to one word per line, and ran off the right-hand edge. It now uses the full width, and scrolls inside its own box rather than making the whole page scroll sideways. |
| 1098 | System            | Improvement | **The import log now says "Job title", not `job_title`.** A line recording a change read `job_title: 1st Line Analyst &rarr; 2nd Line Analyst`, which is the database's name for the field rather than yours. And a person about to be added said only *"Would be created."* &mdash; true, but nothing you can check. A new arrival now lists what their record will actually hold: email, job title, department, office and employee number, or plainly *"No details beyond a name"*, which is itself worth seeing before an import. |
| 1097 | System            | Feature     | **Preview now shows you the people, not just the numbers.** *"31 found, 1 added, 1 updated"* asks to be trusted; this asks to be read. Previewing an import now opens a list of every person it would touch, saying for each one exactly what would happen &mdash; and for a change, **which field, from what, to what**: *"Job title: 1st Line Analyst &rarr; 2nd Line Analyst"*. Filter by what is happening, search by name, and note the wording: a preview says *"Will be added"*, an import that has run says *"Added"*, because labelling something you have not agreed to yet as done is a lie. **Every row of the import history opens the same view**, so a run from three weeks ago answers "updated how, and who?" as readily as the one you just did. The information had been recorded since importing was built &mdash; nothing had ever displayed it. |
| 1096 | System            | Improvement | **A Field mapping tab, with a Test button that reads one real person.** Which detail in your directory becomes which detail in FreeITSM was previously set in two separate places &mdash; four boxes on *Signing in*, seven more on *Importing people* &mdash; which read as two unrelated settings rather than the one map it actually is. They are now on a tab of their own: FreeITSM's field on the left, the directory's attribute on the right. **Test** then reads a single real person and shows the value each row would import, so `employeeID &rarr; NW-1011` replaces an attribute name you had to take on trust. Mistyped attributes are the mistake nobody catches, because nothing fails &mdash; a column is simply empty, and usually nobody notices for weeks. An empty result is ambiguous on its own, so the test also lists **every attribute that person actually carries**, which is what separates "the name is wrong" from "this person has not filled it in". If neither the sign-in name nor the unique id resolves, it says so outright, because an import would skip that person entirely. You can name somebody to check rather than accepting whoever comes first, and nothing is saved and nothing is changed. |
| 1095 | System            | Feature     | **A record of every import, and what it did to whom.** Each run is listed with when it happened, whether it was a preview or the real thing, and how many people were found, added, changed and marked as left &mdash; and behind that, a line per person saying exactly what changed. "47 updated" is a number; this tells you which 47, and how. Previews are logged too, because what somebody was shown before they pressed the button is worth being able to check when the result surprises them. |
| 1094 | System            | Feature     | **Import people from Active Directory or LDAP.** The question that started this: *"how do I import my Active Directory users to assign them the assets?"* Under **System &rarr; Authentication**, a directory can now bring everybody in &mdash; name, email, job title, department, office, phone, employee number and who they report to &mdash; so people exist before they ever sign in. That matters because the staff who hold equipment are largely the staff who never log in at all. **Preview first:** it runs exactly the same job and changes nothing, so you can see precisely what would happen. Nobody is ever deleted; somebody who disappears from the directory is only marked as left after several imports running, and an account disabled in the directory is marked as left here too. **A safety brake stops an import that suddenly finds far fewer people than last time** &mdash; a mistyped starting point or a directory problem looks exactly like everybody leaving at once, and this is what stops that emptying your list. |
| 1093 | Assets            | Improvement | **You can now see who somebody manages, not just who they report to.** A reporting line is stored once, pointing upwards, so the downward view did not exist. A person's details now list the people who report to them, and both the manager and the reports are links &mdash; so you can walk up and down the org chart. People who have left are shown in the list rather than hidden, flagged as such. |
| 1092 | Assets            | Improvement | **The people screen is now a directory, not just a list of who has equipment.** It used to show only people holding something, which made it useless for the job it is most needed for: issuing kit to a new starter, who by definition holds nothing. It now lists people with four views &mdash; **Current people**, **Leavers**, **Everyone**, and **Holding equipment** &mdash; and search covers department, job title and employee number as well as name and email. *Everyone* means everyone, leavers included; *Holding equipment* also includes leavers, because somebody who has left and still has a laptop is the most useful row on the screen. |
| 1091 | Assets            | Feature     | **People records now describe a person, not just a login.** Job title, department, office, phone, mobile, employee number and who they report to can all be recorded, and people can be **added, edited and marked as having left** from **Assets &rarr; Users**. Somebody who has left is never deleted &mdash; they stay on every ticket, asset and handover document they were ever part of, and if they are still holding equipment the screen says so, which is the moment you actually want to know. Office matters more than it looks: the ticket equipment picker searches an asset's location, and this is where that information usually comes from. Groundwork for importing people from Active Directory, but useful on its own with no directory at all. |
| 1090 | System            | Fix         | **A `.git` folder left in the web root was being served.** If FreeITSM was installed by cloning the repository into the web folder &mdash; a common way to do it &mdash; then `/.git/config` and the whole commit history could be downloaded by anyone, on Apache and nginx alike. That file usually contains the address of your repository and sometimes the credentials for it. Nothing blocked it until the new D009 check was written and found it immediately on the development machine. Dotfiles are now refused, with `.well-known` deliberately still served so Let's Encrypt certificates keep renewing. **If your installation predates this, treat anything in `.git/config` as having been readable and change it.** |
| 1089 | System            | Feature     | **A new check: "Guarded paths", under System &rarr; Debug Tools.** Files people upload &mdash; ticket attachments, screen recordings, course content, RFP documents &mdash; are supposed to be reachable only through FreeITSM, which checks who is asking first. Whether that actually holds depends on how the web server was set up, which FreeITSM cannot see. This is the failure that gives you least warning: a wrong setting here does not break anything, it just quietly publishes every attachment, and the first sign of trouble is somebody finding a document they should not have. The check puts a harmless file in each folder, **asks your own server for it exactly as a stranger would**, deletes it again, and tells you plainly what is reachable and what to do about it. It proves it can see your own site before it believes any result, so it can never mistake "unreachable" for "protected". Worth running after installing, after any web server change, and after moving host. |
| 1088 | System            | Fix         | **Signing in briefly landed on a "page not found".** A follow-on from the fix above: the sign-in pages had always been reached at one web address, and sent you to the main screen using a shortcut that assumed it. Once those pages could also be reached at their real address, the shortcut pointed one folder too deep, so signing in succeeded and then showed a 404. Every address those pages send you to is now written out in full, which works from either. |
| 1087 | System            | Improvement | **FreeITSM now ships an nginx configuration**, at `deploy/nginx/freeitsm.conf`, with [a page explaining it](https://github.com/edmozley/freeitsm/wiki/Running-on-nginx). This matters more than convenience: nine of the small server files FreeITSM relies on are **security controls**, and nginx ignores every one of them. Chief among them is the rule that stops ticket attachments being fetched straight from their web address without signing in &mdash; on nginx without this config, they can be, and none of the permission checks in the application are consulted. The config also stops uploaded files ever executing, keeps a `.git` folder out of reach, and applies the session-cookie hardening that PHP-FPM would otherwise miss. The install guide now says plainly that nginx needs it. |
| 1086 | System            | Fix         | **Every page sent a signed-out visitor to a login page that does not exist.** Reported in [issue #68](https://github.com/edmozley/freeitsm/issues/68). The login page moved out of the root folder some time ago, but around ninety files still pointed at the old location. On Apache that was invisible, because a rewrite rule quietly forwarded the old address to the new one. On **nginx, which does not read those rules at all**, a brand-new installation sent every signed-out visitor to a 404 and simply could not be logged into &mdash; which is why it was reported as a missing file. FreeITSM now names the real location everywhere, so it finds its own login page on any web server with no rewriting of any kind. The tidy `/login` address still works exactly as before, and so do existing bookmarks. |
| 1085 | Tickets           | Fix         | **A content search could report more tickets than it listed.** Searching inside tickets for a phrase that also appeared in a knowledge article counted the article in the total but never showed it, because that screen lists tickets and an article is not one &mdash; so "4 tickets found" could appear above three of them. The search now excludes anything that is not attached to a ticket before counting, which also stops those documents taking up result slots a matching ticket could have had. Knowledge articles are still fully searchable from the command palette and the knowledge base, where they belong. |
| 1084 | Tickets           | Fix         | **Attachments on a ticket that arrived by email were never queued for reading, so their contents were never searchable.** A PDF or Word document sent in to the service desk was stored and downloadable as always, but the text inside it was never extracted &mdash; and because it was never even queued, it showed no status at all on **System &rarr; Search**: not read, not pending, not failed, simply absent. That is the one state the status screen cannot report, so nothing indicated anything was wrong. The cause was ordering: a new email ticket announces itself the moment its opening message is stored, which is what prompts indexing, but its attachments are downloaded and saved a moment later &mdash; so when the indexer looked, there was nothing there to find. The ticket is now indexed again once its attachments exist. Attachments added by an analyst or through the portal were never affected. **Existing emailed attachments are picked up automatically** the next time anything happens on their ticket, or immediately via **Rebuild index**. |
| 1083 | Tickets           | Improvement | **The mailbox activity window is much bigger, and its log is far easier to read.** It was a fixed 850 pixels wide with a short list inside, which meant a long sender address and a long subject fought over the same line. It now uses most of the window, and the list grows with your screen instead of showing the same handful of rows on a laptop and a 27-inch monitor. The table itself was the bigger problem: no spacing between columns, so a timestamp ran straight into the sender's name, and no lines between rows. Columns now have sensible fixed widths and proper spacing, long addresses wrap inside their own column rather than shoving everything sideways, each row is separated, and the headings stay put while you scroll. |
| 1082 | Tickets           | Feature     | **An Outbound tab on the mailbox activity view, showing every email FreeITSM has tried to send.** Until now you could see everything that arrived and nothing that left: a successful send appeared in the ticket, and a failed one appeared nowhere at all except a log file on the server. Every one of the eight ways FreeITSM sends email is now recorded &mdash; analyst replies, ticket templates, workflow actions, SLA alerts, portal and system emails, password resets, and shared knowledge articles and change records &mdash; with who it went to, which part of FreeITSM sent it, whether it succeeded, and the provider's own words when it did not. A red count on the tab tells you there are failures without your having to go and look, and sends that never found a mailbox to send from are recorded too, since "nothing could send this" is precisely the failure nobody sees. Prompted by [issue #67](https://github.com/edmozley/freeitsm/issues/67), where ticket acknowledgements were failing every single time and said so only in the server's error log. |
| 1081 | Tickets           | Fix         | **Switching a mailbox between app-only and delegated authentication left the old sign-in token behind.** The two kinds of token are not interchangeable, so the mailbox went on looking authenticated while nothing it sent could succeed &mdash; and because Microsoft rejects the leftover token with the same wording as [issue #67](https://github.com/edmozley/freeitsm/issues/67), it looked exactly like that bug returning rather than a stale credential. Changing the authentication mode, or the target address, now clears the stored token as well as the recorded identity, so the mailbox honestly reports that it needs signing in again. A token of the wrong kind is refused outright if one is somehow still present. Found while testing the fix above; nobody switches modes often, which is why it had gone unnoticed. |
| 1080 | Tickets           | Fix         | **A mailbox set to app-only authentication could not send email at all.** Reported in [issue #67](https://github.com/edmozley/freeitsm/issues/67). Every outgoing message &mdash; workflow email actions, ticket acknowledgements, SLA breach alerts, portal verification emails and password resets &mdash; was addressed to *"the mailbox of whoever signed in"*. That is exactly right for delegated sign-in and meaningless for app-only, where FreeITSM authenticates as itself and nobody signs in, so Microsoft refused every one of them with *"/me request is only valid with delegated authentication flow"*. Messages are now addressed to the mailbox by name. Two further faults were found alongside it and fixed in the same change: the access token for sending was always obtained the delegated way, so even with the address corrected a send would have started failing about an hour after the last mailbox check, with a misleading message about authentication having expired; and a newly configured app-only mailbox was treated as *"no mailbox is configured"* for password resets and portal emails until it had collected mail at least once. **Delegated mailboxes are unaffected** and send exactly as before. |
| 1079 | System            | Improvement | **System &rarr; Search now names the attachments it could not read.** The counts told you something had failed; this tells you *which* file, on which ticket, and why &mdash; so "why can't I find that invoice?" has an answer instead of a shrug. Each one links straight to its ticket. |
| 1078 | System            | Fix         | **Two people using FreeITSM at once no longer means the same document gets read twice.** Documents waiting to be read are now claimed by whichever worker gets there first, so a scheduled run and somebody opening a screen cannot both send the same file to be read &mdash; which mattered most for scanned pages, where reading one is genuinely slow. A worker that dies partway through no longer strands its files either: they return to the queue automatically. Reading a document while somebody waits for a page is also time-limited now, so a big scan can never hold up a screen. |
| 1077 | Tickets           | Improvement | **You decide when documents get read**, under **Tickets &rarr; Settings &rarr; Indexing**. Reading a PDF or a scanned page takes far longer than reading a Word file, so it happens in the background: either on a schedule, or a few at a time while somebody is already using FreeITSM. Both are on to begin with, so attachment searching works on an installation with no scheduled tasks at all, and either can be switched off. |
| 1076 | System            | Feature     | **PDFs, older Office files and scanned documents can now be searched.** Set up a document-reading service under **System &rarr; Integrations &rarr; Apache Tika** and FreeITSM will read the formats it cannot manage on its own &mdash; including running character recognition over scanned pages and photographs, so a picture of an invoice becomes searchable text. There is a **Test connection** button, and switching it on automatically queues everything that could not be read before. FreeITSM does not install or run the service: you point it at one, and the page explains how to start one with a single command. |
| 1075 | Tickets           | Feature     | **Search now looks inside attachments.** Word documents, Excel workbooks, PowerPoint decks and plain text files attached to a ticket are read when they arrive, so a phrase buried in a spreadsheet somebody sent two years ago is findable. Asked for in [discussion #53](https://github.com/edmozley/freeitsm/discussions/53). **PDFs and older Office formats are not read yet** &mdash; those need a separate document-reading service, which is the next piece of work &mdash; and rather than failing quietly, **System &rarr; Search** now lists every attachment by outcome, so you can see exactly which files were read and which could not be. A file is only ever read once, however many times the index is rebuilt. |
| 1074 | System            | Feature     | **A Search screen, under System.** Shows what the search index holds &mdash; how many entries, how many of your tickets and articles are in it, and when it last changed &mdash; and tells you plainly whether anything is missing rather than leaving you to compare two numbers. There is a **Rebuild index** button, so rebuilding no longer needs a command line, which was impossible on hosting that does not give you one. It rebuilds in slices with a progress bar, so a large installation cannot time out halfway and leave the index half-built. The screen also reports the shortest word your database will search for, which is the most common reason for a search that mysteriously finds nothing. |
| 1073 | Knowledge         | Improvement | **Knowledge articles can be found by what is written in them, not just their title.** Until now an article was only findable if you could guess a word in its heading. Search the text and the article turns up, shown under **Found inside articles** in the command palette. Articles are indexed as you save them, including drafts &mdash; you are meant to be able to find your own unfinished work &mdash; and one you send to the recycle bin drops out of search until you restore it. Completes the last part of [discussion #53](https://github.com/edmozley/freeitsm/discussions/53) that was within reach. |
| 1072 | System            | Improvement | **The command palette now searches inside tickets too.** Press **Ctrl+K** (or **&#8984;K**), type a phrase, and as well as matching ticket numbers, subjects, assets and articles by name, it finds tickets whose *messages or notes* contain what you typed &mdash; shown separately under **Found inside tickets** so it is clear why a ticket with an unrelated-looking subject is in the list. Asked for in [discussion #53](https://github.com/edmozley/freeitsm/discussions/53). Content matches are listed after the name matches and capped, so typing a hostname still takes you straight to that machine rather than burying it under message snippets. |
| 1071 | Tickets           | Improvement | **Search now keeps itself up to date.** Searching inside tickets used to rely on somebody running a script by hand, so anything raised since the last run simply could not be found &mdash; which is worse than having no search at all, because you trust it and stop looking. Tickets, replies and notes are now indexed the moment they happen, and a ticket sent to the trash drops out of the index straight away. The rebuild script is still there for repairs and for the first run on an existing installation. |
| 1070 | Tickets           | Fix         | **A ticket raised in the portal, or one that arrived by email, never announced that it had been created.** Only tickets raised by an analyst did. Anything listening was therefore blind to the two channels most tickets actually arrive through: **a workflow triggered on "ticket created" never ran for them**, and they never reached the notification bell. All three routes now announce identically. **Worth checking your workflows after updating** &mdash; a rule that has quietly never fired for emailed tickets will start working, which is the fix, but it will look like new behaviour. |
| 1069 | Assets            | Fix         | **The inventory script's help pointed at a menu that does not exist.** The deployment guide said to generate the API key in *Admin &rarr; API Keys*, which is nowhere in FreeITSM, so anyone following it step by step arrived at a dead end. It now says **Software &rarr; Settings &rarr; API Keys**, and warns that this is not the same thing as the keys under **System &rarr; API** &mdash; those belong to the REST API, begin `fitsm_`, and will never authenticate the script no matter how valid they are. A key from the wrong page fails with *Invalid authorization key*, which reads like an expired key rather than the wrong kind of key. |
| 1068 | Tickets           | Improvement | **Equipment and CMDB objects now sit in the Links bar rather than in panels of their own.** They are links like a problem, a change or a related ticket, so they belong where you already look for what a ticket is connected to — and both are attached from the same **Link to…** menu as everything else. The two sections they replaced took a bordered panel each whether or not anything was in them, so an ordinary ticket spent most of a screen saying "nothing here yet" twice. Equipment and configuration items are still shown distinctly, because they are not the same kind of thing: a broken mouse is an asset and will never be a configuration item. |
| 1067 | Self-Service      | Feature     | **People can say which of their devices a ticket is about.** When raising a ticket in the portal there is now a **Which equipment is this about?** dropdown listing the kit assigned to them, so "my monitor is flickering" arrives naming the monitor, with its model and serial already attached. The field only appears if they actually have equipment assigned, and only ever lists their own. Shared items such as a meeting room screen or a printer are not listed — nobody is assigned those, so the requester describes it as they do today and an analyst attaches it. |
| 1066 | Assets            | Feature     | **A Tickets tab on every asset, showing what has been reported against it.** Open tickets first, then everything that came before, so you can see at a glance that a monitor has failed three times this year rather than treating each report as the first. Until now nothing connected tickets and assets in either direction. |
| 1065 | Tickets           | Feature     | **Equipment can be linked to a ticket.** Asked for in [discussion #57](https://github.com/edmozley/freeitsm/discussions/57). An **Affected equipment** section on the ticket shows each item's asset tag, make and model, serial number, type and location, so the device is identified without a round of questions. The picker opens showing the equipment assigned to the person who raised it — usually the right answer — and searching finds anything in the estate, **including by location**, which is how you find a meeting room screen that nobody owns and whose hostname nobody knows. |
| 1064 | Tickets           | Fix         | **Merging two tickets left the CMDB objects behind on the old one.** The merge is documented to carry linked configuration items across to the surviving ticket, and every other linked record — problems, changes, notes, tasks, time entries — did move. The CMDB step alone referred to a column by the wrong name, and the resulting database error was being swallowed by error handling meant for installations where the table doesn't exist yet, so the move simply never happened and nothing was reported. Nothing was lost, since a merged ticket is never deleted, but the links stayed where you would not think to look for them. |
| 1063 | Assets            | Improvement | **The inventory script can pin the server's certificate.** Where there is no internal CA to install, `-CertificateThumbprint` tells the script exactly which certificate to expect, and the inventory is sent only if the server presents that one &mdash; so a self-signed certificate no longer means choosing between "doesn't work" and "checks nothing". Paste the thumbprint straight from certmgr or a browser; spaces, colons and lower case are all accepted. `-SkipCertificateCheck` remains for lab use, and now says plainly that it exposes the API key. |
| 1062 | Assets            | Fix         | **The inventory script could not post to a FreeITSM using a self-signed certificate.** Machines that did not trust the certificate stopped with *"Could not establish trust relationship for the SSL/TLS secure channel"* and no inventory ever arrived &mdash; with nothing in the message to say what was wrong or what to do about it. The script now explains the failure and offers three fixes in order of safety, and it asks for TLS 1.2 explicitly on Windows PowerShell 5.1, which otherwise still offers TLS 1.0 and is refused outright by a hardened server. A bad `-CertificateThumbprint` is also caught before the inventory is collected rather than after, saving the best part of a minute per attempt. |
| 1061 | Assets            | Improvement | **The handover document can be emailed straight to the person.** Sent through the mailbox FreeITSM already uses, with the document laid out in the body of the message rather than as an attachment, so it can be read on a phone without downloading anything. |
| 1060 | Assets            | Feature     | **You can design the handover document yourself**, under **Assets &rarr; Settings &rarr; Handover document**. Switch sections on or off, reorder them, reword them, and choose which columns the equipment table shows. Merge codes such as `{{employee.name}}`, `{{asset_count}}` and `{{date}}` fill themselves in when a document is produced, and a live preview shows exactly what will come out as you type. Keep several templates — an onboarding pack and a leaver's checklist, say — and mark one as the default. |
| 1059 | Assets            | Feature     | **A printable handover document for any person.** Lists who they are, every item they hold with its serial number, asset tag and assignment date, a declaration that the equipment remains the organisation's property, and a place for both the employee and IT to sign. Your company logo appears on it if one is set under **System &rarr; Branding**. Print it, or use your browser's **Save as PDF** for an electronic copy. |
| 1058 | Assets            | Feature     | **A Users tab showing who holds what.** Asked for in [discussion #56](https://github.com/edmozley/freeitsm/discussions/56). Pick somebody and see everything assigned to them on one screen &mdash; type, name, make and model, serial number, asset tag and when it was assigned &mdash; instead of searching the asset list one item at a time. Useful for onboarding, hardware swaps, audits and offboarding. |
| 1057 | Workflows         | Feature     | **Two new triggers: a note is added to a ticket, and a requester replies.** Added while building the notification bell, but useful on their own — until now nothing announced that somebody had said something on a ticket, so no workflow could act on it. A reply is recognised from both the portal and inbound email, and only when it is a reply, never the message that opened the ticket. |
| 1056 | Tickets           | Fix         | **Replying from the self-service portal now announces itself properly.** The portal reply loaded only the ticket's number and subject, so nothing downstream could tell who the ticket belonged to. |
| 1055 | System            | Improvement | **You choose which events reach your bell**, under **Preferences &rarr; Notifications**. Sensible ones are on to begin with: assignments, replies, notes, status and priority changes on your tickets, and SLA warnings. Anything you do not want is one switch away, and it is your setting alone. |
| 1054 | System            | Feature     | **A notification bell now sits in the header on every screen.** Asked for in [discussion #55](https://github.com/edmozley/freeitsm/discussions/55). It shows what has happened on the tickets assigned to you — a reply from the requester, a colleague's note, an assignment, a status or priority change, an SLA warning — with a count of what you have not read, and a click takes you straight to the ticket. **It is built to stay switched on.** You are never told about your own actions, several changes to the same ticket are grouped into one entry rather than several, and a bulk update of fifty tickets produces no notifications instead of fifty. |
