| 1053 | System            | Fix         | **The logo picker offered SVG files the server would refuse.** SVG was dropped when the upload rules were tightened in the security round, but the file picker still listed it and the help text still recommended it for crisp printing — so choosing one got you an error message instead of a greyed-out file. Both now say PNG or JPG. |
| 1052 | System            | Fix         | **A rejected Branding save no longer blanks the header and footer text on its way out.** The page saved the six text slots before it had finished checking the rest of the request, so a save refused for any reason still wiped them. Everything is now checked before anything is written. |
| 1051 | System            | Feature     | **You can choose which page people land on when they open FreeITSM.** Asked for in [discussion #63](https://github.com/edmozley/freeitsm/discussions/63). Previously the address always went to the analyst login, which is an odd front door on an installation where most people are end users. **System &rarr; Branding** now sets it to either the analyst login or the self-service portal, and analysts can override the choice for themselves under **Preferences &rarr; Start page** so nobody gains an extra click. Both login pages link to each other, so neither is ever out of reach. Your own choice is remembered in your account and reapplied whenever you sign in, including on a new computer. |
| 1050 | Morning Checks    | Improvement | **The in-app help guide has been brought up to date.** It gains a section on groups and routing, and several things it had been getting wrong are corrected: it described Green, Amber and Red as fixed when statuses are fully configurable, said Amber and Red always require a note when that is a per-status setting, and documented only one of the four settings tabs. It now also covers the Statuses tab, the Groups tab, the Chart tab, and the tool for remapping results whose status was deleted. |
| 1049 | Morning Checks    | Fix         | **Changing a check's status no longer throws away the note without asking.** If a check had a note against it and you clicked a status that does not carry one, the note was deleted silently — and the note is usually the only record of *why* a check went amber. FreeITSM now asks first, naming the status you are moving to, and you can cancel. |
| 1048 | Morning Checks    | Fix         | **A check completed by somebody covering was credited to the wrong person.** The round recorded whoever set a status *first* and never updated it, so if a colleague was off and someone else redid the check, the board still thanked the colleague. It now records who set the status that is actually showing. |
| 1047 | Morning Checks    | Improvement | **You can put a check back to not checked.** Clicking the wrong colour used to be permanent — there was no way back to a blank row short of editing the database. There is now an undo beside each completed check. It asks first, because clearing a check also discards the note and the attribution that came with it. |
| 1046 | Morning Checks    | Improvement | **The round now shows who checked each item and when**, in their own columns, so a glance at the board answers "has anyone actually done this?" without opening anything. The completed-by information was already being recorded — it had simply never been shown. |
| 1045 | Morning Checks    | Feature     | **You can raise a ticket or a task straight from a morning check.** The check's name, status and notes are pre-filled, and the check keeps a record of what it raised. Raising something is deliberately *not* undone by clearing the check afterwards, because correcting a mis-click should not quietly close a real piece of work. |
| 1044 | Morning Checks    | Feature     | **Checks can now be grouped, and groups routed to a team or an analyst.** Asked for in [discussion #64](https://github.com/edmozley/freeitsm/discussions/64). Groups are optional — an installation that never makes one sees no change. A group can point at a team or a named analyst, and an individual check can override that with an analyst of its own. **Routing is guidance, never permission**: anyone with access to Morning Checks can still complete any check, so the round still gets done when somebody calls in sick. A **Mine** filter appears once anything is routed, and stays hidden otherwise. |
| 1043 | Service Status    | Improvement | **Incidents now keep a running thread of updates.** Each time you save an incident FreeITSM records what changed — the status, the comment, who made the change, and which services were at which impact level at that moment. Open **Updates** beside any incident to read it back. Previously the comment box held only the latest text, overwriting whatever was there before. |
| 1042 | Service Status    | Fix         | **Bringing services back one at a time is now recorded properly.** If a service was on Major Outage and you moved it to Degraded, or took it off the incident because it had recovered, the earlier state was overwritten — so the history reported the whole incident at whatever level it happened to end on, and a service restored on day one looked as though it had been down for the full three days. Each save now records a timestamped snapshot, so a three-day incident affecting four services gives each of them its own accurate downtime. |
| 1041 | Service Status    | Improvement | **Each impact level now says whether time at that level counts as downtime.** Set on the level itself, over on **Status &rarr; Settings &rarr; Impact levels**, so a level you add later is asked the question when you create it rather than needing a separate rules page to be kept in step. Planned maintenance is excluded by default, because counting it makes a well-run service look worse than a neglected one. |
| 1040 | Service Status    | Feature     | **Every service now has a history and an uptime figure.** Asked for in [discussion #59](https://github.com/edmozley/freeitsm/discussions/59). Open **History and uptime** on any service to see a day-by-day strip for the last 7, 30, 90 or 365 days, the percentage of that period the service was up, and every incident that touched it with how long it lasted. **It works on outages that have already happened** — the history is worked out from your existing incidents rather than starting from the day you upgrade, so a service you have been running for a year has a year of history immediately. **Status &rarr; Settings &rarr; Uptime** sets the default period and whether customers see the figures in the portal, which is off to begin with. |
| 1039 | Tickets           | Fix         | **The requester list was not limited to the companies you can see.** On installations hosting more than one customer company, the list of people used when raising a ticket, and on the Users screen, returned every requester on the whole installation, complete with email addresses — regardless of which companies the analyst was allowed to work with. Only the ticket count beside each name was being limited, which made it look careful while the names themselves were not. It is now limited to your active company, the same way tickets, assets and changes already are. Found while building the requester picker below, which would have made that list far easier to browse. |
| 1038 | Tickets           | Feature     | **You can now search for a requester when raising a ticket instead of typing their name and email every time.** Asked for in [discussion #54](https://github.com/edmozley/freeitsm/discussions/54). Start typing a name or an email address and pick the person from the list — their company is shown beside them so you can tell two similar names apart. If they are not on the system yet, **Add someone new** is always the last option in the list, and it keeps whatever you had already typed rather than making you start again. There is also a magnifier beside the box if you would rather browse the full list than search it. Two long-standing quirks go with it: the name box used to be silently ignored whenever the person already existed, and a typo in the email address used to create a second, duplicate person without saying anything. |
| 1037 | Tickets           | Feature     | **Your ticket list can now show priority, status and who owns each ticket — and you choose how much of that you want to see.** Asked for in [discussion #61](https://github.com/edmozley/freeitsm/discussions/61). Each of the three can be turned on independently and shown in whichever form suits you: a coloured bar down the **left edge** of the row, a small **block in the top right**, a **pill with the word in it**, or just a **dot** — and the agent as a full name or as initials. **Tickets &rarr; Settings &rarr; Row display** has a live preview so you can see a real row change as you pick, rather than guessing. It is your own setting and changes nothing for anyone else; administrators can additionally set the default for everyone who has not chosen. The original request was to replace the message preview line with the assignee's name — that line is deliberately kept, because it is the only clue on the row about what the ticket actually says. |
| 1036 | Tasks             | Fix         | **A busy database could briefly let one company see another company's tasks.** The check deciding whether you may reach a ticket's tasks answered "yes" whenever its database query failed for any reason at all. That was meant to keep part-migrated installations working, and it did — but it also treated a momentary lock, a dropped connection or a permissions error the same way. The failure would only appear under load, leave no trace, and never reproduce on a quiet system. It now allows only the case it was written for, and refuses and logs everything else. |
| 1035 | System            | Improvement | **Database Verification now tells you what it will change before it changes it, and stops claiming it never deletes anything.** The page has a new **Preview** button that inspects your database and reports exactly what a verification would create, add or **permanently remove** — without touching anything. It matters because the note inside the code said verification "never drops anything", and that was not true: it removes seven outdated columns once their contents have been copied somewhere better. Anyone who read that note had no reason to take a backup first. The page now says plainly that verification changes your database, and the preview names every item that would go and why. |
| 1034 | System            | Fix         | **A logo can no longer be uploaded as an SVG, and the file is stored under a name FreeITSM chooses.** An SVG is not really a picture — it is a document that can contain a program, and because the logo is served from your own web address, anybody who opened the logo file directly would have run that program as though FreeITSM had sent it. Every other part of FreeITSM had already stopped accepting SVGs for this reason; the branding screen had its own separate list and never got the message. PNG and JPG are unaffected. **If you already use an SVG logo it keeps working, but replacing it with a PNG is worth doing.** |
| 1033 | Multiple          | Fix         | **Uploaded files are refused, rather than trusted, when the server cannot inspect them.** FreeITSM checks that a file's contents match its name, so a program renamed to `.png` is caught. On a server missing a standard PHP component that check quietly did nothing at all and the file was accepted on the strength of its name — the weaker of the two checks, doing the work of both. It now refuses the upload and tells the administrator which component to switch on. |
| 1032 | System            | Fix         | **The sign-in page and the setup page no longer announce your exact PHP version to strangers.** The setup page is reachable without signing in, by necessity, and it printed the precise version of PHP you are running — which is the single most useful thing to know when looking for a way in, because it maps directly to a published list of weaknesses. It now shows whether your version is fine, old, or too old, without the number; sign in as an administrator to see it. Every other page was quietly announcing the same thing in a hidden header, which has also been removed. |
| 1031 | Tickets           | Fix         | **The conversation snapshot saved when tickets are merged is now stored safely like every other attachment.** Merging kept a copy of the closed ticket's conversation as a web page filed in the attachments folder, written directly rather than going through the checks every other attachment passes. It is now stored under a random name in a form no web server will ever run. You still download and open the same readable file — nothing about the feature changes. |
| 1030 | Security          | Fix         | **Guessing a two-factor code five times now locks the code step for everybody, not just for that browser tab.** The five-attempt limit was remembered in the visitor's own session, which is the one thing an attacker can throw away. Signing in again with a valid password handed out five fresh attempts — and because a correct password also clears the ordinary lockout counters, someone who already knew a password could keep guessing six-digit codes indefinitely at a cost of one extra request per five tries. The count now lives on the account, survives signing in again, and is cleared only by entering a correct code. It applies to analyst and customer-portal sign-in alike. |
| 1029 | Multiple          | Fix         | **Four more places where one customer company could reach another's data are closed.** Following the August security review: deleting a customer contact checked nothing at all and would say how many tickets that contact had before refusing — enough to count another company's workload without ever being allowed to touch it; the REST API could list, read and modify any requester on the install regardless of which company a key was issued to; the "preview before escalating" step returned another company's subject, requester, message and attachment names because the company check lived in the code that the preview stops short of; and the two messaging diagnostic screens would test a channel belonging to a company the analyst cannot see. In every case the refusal is now identical to the one for something that does not exist, so nobody can learn what they are not allowed to see. |
| 1028 | Self-service      | Fix         | **Changing your portal password now ends any other session using your account.** That is usually the whole reason somebody changes it in a hurry: they think someone else is signed in as them. The password did change, but the other session carried on working, so the one thing the user was trying to achieve was the one thing that did not happen. It failed quietly — nothing was logged and the screen said the change had succeeded, because the code that renews your session was being called at a point where it could not do anything. The equivalent screen for analysts was always correct. |
| 1027 | Multiple          | Feature     | **Voice notes, video and phone photos now come through as attachments, and you can choose which file types you accept.** The list of accepted attachment types was written for email and quietly governed the chat channels too, so nine of the file types WhatsApp, Slack and web chat actually send — voice notes, video, iPhone photos, shared contacts — were being set aside as unrecognised by the very feature built to receive them. Audio, video, HEIC photos and the files Outlook staples to ordinary mail (calendar invites, forwarded messages, `winmail.dat`) are now accepted. **System &rarr; Security** gains a box listing the types you accept: leave it empty to take everything FreeITSM considers safe, including anything added by future updates, or name just the types you want. You can only narrow the list — typing a program or script extension into it does nothing, because nothing outside the safe set can be enabled from a text box. |
| 1026 | Knowledge         | Fix         | **Sharing an article by email works again.** The mail server password is now stored encrypted, and the part of the code that reads it back had not been told, so it was handing the mail server the encrypted text instead of the password. Sending failed with an authentication error that pointed nowhere near the real cause. Saving the settings screen stored the password unencrypted again, so the problem came and went depending on which had happened most recently. The password is also no longer sent back to the settings screen at all — it shows as dots. |
| 1025 | System            | Fix         | **The webhook cron address you are told to copy is a working one again.** Cron tokens are now encrypted where they are stored, and this screen was still reading them raw, so the address it offered contained the encrypted text and the server answered "forbidden" to an administrator following our own instructions. The scheduled jobs themselves were never affected. There is also a new command, `php scripts/cron_token.php`, that prints the real tokens — the setup guides used to tell you to read them straight out of the database, which no longer gives you anything usable. |
| 1024 | System            | Fix         | **Signing in with single sign-on no longer skips a required password change.** An account told to change its password at next sign-in was held to that everywhere except through SSO, which let it straight through. It matters because the reason for the flag is usually that the account still has a widely-published default password — and that password keeps working on the ordinary sign-in page no matter how the person arrived this time. |
| 1023 | System            | Fix         | **Database Verification can no longer overwrite one attachment with another.** When it renames old attachments to a safe extension, two files on the same email could end up wanting the same new name — `report.htm` and `report.html`, for instance. The second quietly replaced the first, and both records then pointed at the survivor, so one attachment was gone for good. It now finds a free name instead. The same pass also recognises several more risky extensions than it used to. |
| 1022 | System            | Fix         | **The Docker quickstart now forces the default password to be changed, as the guide always said it would.** On that route the admin account was created by the database file rather than by Database Verification, and only the second of those two set the "must change password at first sign-in" flag — so on the most-used install path the published `admin` / `freeitsm` password stayed valid indefinitely. Both routes now set it, and Database Verification will also flag an existing admin account that is still using the published password. Accounts whose password has already been changed are left alone. |
| 1021 | System            | Fix         | **A brief database hiccup can no longer switch off the checks that keep companies apart.** Those checks begin by asking "does this install have more than one company?", and if that single question failed for any reason — a locked table, a dropped connection — the answer came back "no", every check downstream stood down, and it stayed that way for the rest of that page load. Only a genuinely missing table now means "one company"; anything else is treated as "assume more than one" so the checks still run. Companion to the fix in the previous release, which corrected the checks themselves but not the question in front of them. |
| 1020 | Tickets           | Fix         | **An analyst can no longer create a customer contact belonging to a company they cannot see.** The check that stops somebody filing a person into another company only ran when the request actually named a company. Leaving it out skipped the check altogether, and FreeITSM then worked the company out from the email address — so a contact could be created inside another company, with a chosen password, and signed in as. The check now runs against the company the contact will really end up in, whether it was named or worked out. Single-company installs are unaffected. |
| 1019 | Multiple          | Improvement | **German is being brought up to date — from 47% to 58% of the interface so far.** German had fallen a long way behind, though it turned out not to be a German problem: fifteen languages sit at exactly the same point, all missing the same seven modules, so a whole tier stopped being maintained at once. Now translated for German: the **first-run setup page** (the one screen where an untranslated word costs you a reader before they have even logged in), the whole **self-service portal** (customer-facing, so its readers are the least likely to shrug at English), the **war room**, the **system wiki**, and the **System area's home page** along with branding, colours, database verification, debug tools, demo data, encryption, module access and preferences. Terminology was taken from the seventeen German files that already existed rather than decided afresh, because a new file that disagrees with the old ones is worse than no file at all: formal address throughout, and *Ticket*, *Asset*, *Analyst* and *Workflow* left in English because that is what German IT actually says. This also settled a question that had been open since the Norwegian work — whether to write *AI* or *KI* — by counting: German already uses **KI** 91 times, and all three uses of *AI* are in code comments no user ever sees. Verified by loading the pages in German and confirming no untranslated placeholders appear. Still to do: contracts, the network mapper, the rest of System, and around 2,600 individual strings in modules that are otherwise translated. |
| 1018 | War room          | Fix         | **Warbot said "no AI provider is configured" when one was.** The provider was working perfectly and every call succeeded. Warbot reads the last few messages of the channel so it can follow on from what was just said — and that channel was still full of its own earlier replies from before a provider had been set up, so it simply copied one. The giveaway was that the wording was subtly not ours: a capital letter we do not use and a differently formatted list. Warbot's own past messages are now clearly marked as its own rather than presented as house style, they are shortened so there is no wall of text worth copying, and an old "I cannot reach my provider" notice is left out of what it reads entirely &mdash; if it is answering at all, that message cannot be true. |
| 1017 | War room          | Fix         | **The × on the search and situation-report panel did nothing, and the settings tabs did not switch.** Two separate faults with the same cause: something that worked while there was only one of it. The panel's close button had always been wired up, but a styling rule was quietly overriding the instruction to hide it, so it stayed on screen no matter what. And the war room settings page had only ever had a single tab &mdash; and a single tab is always the one showing &mdash; so nothing had ever needed to switch between them; adding the situation-report tab is what revealed that the switching had never been written. A third, unnoticed instance of the first fault was also fixed: the row that lists files you have attached was holding an empty strip of space under the message box even when there were none. |
| 1016 | System            | Improvement | **A command that tells you how far behind each translation has fallen.** A locale does not announce that it is out of date: a missing string quietly falls back to English and renders perfectly, so a half-translated module looks finished right up until somebody who actually reads that language opens it. With English still growing and twenty-three other languages not growing with it, the only way to know is to compare all 9,290 strings, which is not something anyone does by hand twice. `php scripts/i18n_audit.php --all` prints a coverage percentage for every language, worst first; naming one language shows the detail. It reports whole modules that have no translation file at all, individual missing strings, keys left behind from an older version of English, and how many strings are still byte-for-byte identical to the English. It also checks **placeholders in both directions**, which is the part that matters most: a translation that loses a `{name}` or swaps two `%s` markers is worse than one that is simply missing, because it renders rather than falling back, so nobody ever reports it &mdash; it just prints the wrong value, or a raw token, at the user. Read-only, and documented in the wiki. |
| 1015 | War room          | Feature     | **Warbot learns six new things to look up, and most of them were already in your database going unread.** **Known errors** &mdash; the root causes and workarounds recorded in Problem Management, which is the highest-value question in an incident and the one nobody thinks to go and check at three in the morning; Warbot now quotes the workaround in full. **Ticket surge** &mdash; how many tickets have come in over the last hour compared with the usual rate *for that time of day*, which tells the room something nobody in it knows yet; comparing against a flat daily average would call every weekday morning a spike. **Who to ring** &mdash; the supplier behind a service, their contract and end date, and their people with direct dials, switchboard, mobiles and email, because "who do we call about Exchange" at 3am is a real problem with a real answer sitting in Contracts. **Morning checks** &mdash; what this morning's checks said and which were not clear, since an incident at half nine is often something the eight o'clock check already caught. **Search the war room itself** &mdash; what did we already say about this, for the person who joins an hour in. **Linked tickets** &mdash; the duplicates and children of a ticket, to find out whether five reports are one problem. All six are read-only and run on your own server, so like the rest of Warbot's lookups they keep working when the internet does not: `/known`, `/spike`, `/supplier`, `/checks`, `/find` and `/linked`. Two smaller fixes came with them &mdash; the command list Warbot prints is now built from the commands themselves rather than typed out separately, so it can no longer go stale, and commands that take an optional value (`/checks 2026-07-04`, `/changes 30`) now actually use it instead of quietly ignoring it and answering about today. |
| 1014 | System            | Feature     | **A new check that tells you the war room will work before the day you need it.** System &rarr; Debug Tools gains **D008 &mdash; War room health**. Every other module tells you it is broken the moment you try to use it; the war room is opened for the first time *during* an incident, when the usual chat is already down and nobody has any appetite for discovering that the attachments folder is unwritable or that the all-hands channel was never created. So this checks the things that fail silently: the seven tables, the **delete rules that differ on purpose** &mdash; above all that removing an analyst leaves the conversation intact, since a wrong rule there does nothing at all until somebody is deleted and then quietly destroys the record of an incident &mdash; whether any pair of analysts has ended up with two message threads, the attachments folder and both of its protection files, files left on disk with no record and records whose file has gone, whether message retention is keeping up, and how many languages have been translated. It **runs one of Warbot's lookups for real** rather than reporting that it is installed, because a lookup whose query names a column that does not exist returns nothing rather than failing. It finishes with an end-to-end test &mdash; post a message, read it back, record who is here &mdash; written inside a transaction and rolled back, so nothing ever appears in somebody's open war room. Ends in a plain-English verdict: all good, or a numbered list of problems each with what to do. |
| 1013 | War room          | Improvement | **The war room gets its help guide, and its colours.** The module now has the same illustrated guide every other module has, reached from Help in its own menu: what it is for, the four kinds of channel and how they differ, mentioning people and the bell that follows you around FreeITSM, attaching files, editing and deleting, searching, Warbot and its commands, the situation report, and which settings belong to an administrator versus to you. It is written for somebody opening the war room for the first time *because* something is broken, so it leads with what still works when nothing else does. Also fixes something invisible: the module had been drawing its amber from a colour that **was never actually defined** &mdash; every use carried a hard-coded fallback, so it looked right by accident and never adapted to dark mode. The colour is now a proper theme value with a lighter shade for dark backgrounds. |
| 1012 | War room          | Feature     | **Warbot &mdash; an assistant that sits in the war room and looks things up for you.** Mention it (`@Warbot how many P1s are open?`) and it answers, in the channel, where everyone can see. It can tell you the open tickets at any priority, which services are degraded and what is being published to customers, **what changed recently**, who is on call, details of a machine by hostname or asset tag, what depends on a configuration item, and whether there is a runbook for something. *What changed recently* is the one that earns its place: it is usually the first useful question in an incident, and it matches on when the work or outage was scheduled rather than when the change was written up &mdash; so a change raised three weeks ago and carried out at six this morning is the one it finds. **It keeps working when the internet does not.** The lookups are ordinary database queries that run on your own server; only the plain-English understanding needs an AI provider. So when the provider cannot be reached &mdash; which during a real outage is likely &mdash; Warbot says so plainly and the commands still work: `/p1`, `/status`, `/changes`, `/oncall`, `/asset`, `/impact`, `/kb`, `/help`. A bot that goes quiet during the incident it exists for would be worse than no bot at all. **It can only read, never change anything**, which is deliberate: anyone in the room can type instructions at it, so the limit is built into what it is able to do rather than into what it has been asked not to do. Its answers are operational &mdash; counts, states, hostnames &mdash; and it will not read a ticket out to a room; it points you at the ticket instead. | 951 | Integrations      | Feature     | **The issue status on a ticket now keeps itself up to date.** A new scheduled task (`cron/integration_poll.php`) asks each configured tracker what has happened to the issues FreeITSM is linked to, and updates the pill on the ticket — so when a developer moves something to Done, the service desk can see it without asking. **This is currently the only thing that updates status**, since inbound webhooks are a later slice, so the setup guide (`docs/integration-poll-cron-setup.md`) opens by saying that plainly: schedule it or nothing ever changes. Escalation is driven by a workflow, and workflow conditions are editable by anyone who can author workflows — so without a hardcoded check, one mis-scoped rule could push Acme's ticket content into Globex's Jira. The check now lives in code that nobody can edit, runs before any network call or database write, and treats an unrouted ticket as the Default company's rather than guessing. On a single-company install it is trivially always true, which is correct rather than a bypass — there is only one company for anything to leak to. **Also**: a schema gate so an install that has not run Database Verification yet sees "no linked issues" instead of an error (a missing gate of exactly this kind once produced an empty inbox); the admin connection list returns `has_credentials` as a boolean and **never** the stored token, which is what makes an install-wide list safe; dry run returns a preview *before* the network call, so testing a workflow can never mint a real Jira issue; and the status refresh batches every link on a connection into one query, writing only rows that actually moved, so a quiet day costs one read and no writes. Only a change of status *category* is treated as an event worth acting on — a rename from "In Progress" to "In progress" should not wake anybody up. **Tests**: 151 total. The guard has 15 of its own, and every "cannot escalate across companies" assertion is paired with a "can escalate within one" — a guard that refused everything would otherwise pass the whole negative half while being completely broken. Verified both ways by deliberate breakage: made permissive, exactly the 5 refusal tests fail; made refuse-everything, exactly the 10 permission tests fail. |
| 946 | Integrations      | Feature     | **The Jira connector — the first tracker to plug into the new engine.** Still nothing visible in the app; this is the piece that actually talks to Jira. It handles **both Jira Cloud and Jira Data Center / Server**, which sound like the same product but are not: Cloud uses REST v3 and wants descriptions as ADF (a nested JSON document), Data Center uses v2 and wants wiki markup, Cloud authenticates with an email plus API token while Data Center uses a Personal Access Token, and Cloud identifies people by an account id where Data Center uses a username. Rather than two connectors with most of their code duplicated, it is one connector with a *flavour* that is detected once when you test the connection — and if the guess is wrong (a vanity domain in front of Cloud, say) it tries the other rather than reporting bad credentials. **Three decisions worth recording.** The ticket's priority is deliberately **not** mapped onto Jira's priority field, because Jira priorities are per-project with arbitrary names and sending one fails on any project that renamed them — priority travels as text in the description instead, until V3 where an admin says explicitly which name means which. Jira's error responses are unpacked properly, so the most common real failure ("this project requires an Epic Link") names the field and the reason rather than saying "HTTP 400". And if the issue is created successfully but the follow-up read of its status fails, the issue still exists, so the link is kept with an unknown status rather than the whole escalation being thrown away. Batch status refresh uses a single JQL query for the whole watch list rather than one call per ticket, since that is the poll cron's hot path, and non-numeric ids are rejected before they can reach the query. **Tests**: 70 further assertions (136 total in `tests/integrations/run.php`), all without a live Jira — the network layer is stubbed so payload shape, the ADF-vs-wiki choice, status mapping, error extraction, project paging, auth headers and the flavour fallback are all provable offline. Verified again by deliberate breakage; that exercise also found an assertion that would have crashed the suite instead of failing it, which is now fixed. |
| 945 | Integrations      | Feature     | **Groundwork for linking tickets to external issue trackers — Jira first, then GitHub, GitLab and Azure DevOps.** Nothing is visible in the app yet; this is the engine the feature is built on. The problem it solves is the one every service desk has: a ticket arrives, an analyst realises it's actually a bug for the dev team, and today that means copy-pasting into Jira and remembering to check back. Two new tables land — `integration_connections` (a configured Jira site or GitHub org, credentials encrypted at rest) and `integration_links` (the ticket ↔ issue spine). Plus two new files under `includes/integrations/`: `IssueTrackerProvider`, the provider-agnostic contract every tracker plugs into — deliberately the same shape as `MessagingProvider`, which already puts Twilio and Meta Cloud behind one door — and `IssueDoc`, which solves the awkward bit. Every tracker wants a different body format (Jira Cloud wants ADF, a nested JSON document; Jira Data Center wants wiki markup; GitHub and GitLab want Markdown; Azure DevOps wants HTML), so rather than four sets of string-building that drift apart, the description is **built once as a document and rendered per provider**. That's why adding a second tracker later is one file rather than a rewrite. **Two decisions worth recording.** `integration_connections` is a *connection*-shaped table for multi-company purposes — `tenant_id` NULL means **shared across every company** (an MSP's own Jira), set means **pinned** to one client — which is the same convention as mailboxes and messaging channels, and the **opposite** of tickets, where NULL means the Default company. Scoping it with `activeTenantFilter()` would hide every shared connection from every client. And `status_category` (todo / in progress / done / cancelled) is stored alongside the raw status name because Jira statuses are per-project and freely renamed: every decision keys off the category, never the name — the same lesson as `tickets.merged_into_id`. **Tests**: `tests/integrations/run.php`, 66 assertions covering all four renderers, escaping (a requester writing "use the * wildcard" must not produce italics, and `<script>` must not survive into an Azure DevOps description), degenerate documents that would otherwise make Jira reject the whole request, and the provider contract itself. Each negative assertion is paired with a positive control, and the suite was verified to actually fail when the escaper is deliberately broken. |
| 944 | Forms             | Feature     | **Forms can finally ask for a date properly.** Until now there was no date field at all, so every "when do you need this by?", "first day off", "when did the error start?" had to be a plain text box with the format begged for in the label — and people typed *14/8*, *next Tuesday*, *asap* anyway. There is now a proper **Date / time** field with a real calendar (or clock) picker, and it's **one field with a setting** rather than three separate types: choose whether it asks for **a date**, **a time**, or **date and time**, and change your mind later. That matters because a field's type can't be changed once it exists — with three separate types, realising a month in that you needed the time too would mean deleting the question and starting its column again, stranding every answer already given. A setting is just a setting. Dates work with conditional questions too, with **is before** / **is after** tests — so *"first day off is before 1 September"* can reveal a "why the short notice?" box only when it's actually needed. The AI assistant now knows about date fields as well, and has stopped being told to fake them as text (it used to be instructed to produce a text box labelled *"Start date (DD/MM/YYYY)"* — that instruction is gone). It also learned about section headings, which it was allowed to use since the last release but was never actually told existed. **One deliberate detail worth knowing:** a date on a form is stored and shown exactly as the person typed it, with **no timezone conversion**. Most dates in FreeITSM are moments in time and get converted into each viewer's own timezone — but "I need this by the 14th" means the 14th to everyone, and an analyst in another country reading it as the 13th would be a bug, not a feature. |
| 943 | Forms             | Fix         | **Form submissions are now properly restricted to analysts with Forms access.** Every write endpoint in the Forms module checked that the analyst could actually use the module; the endpoint that returns **submission contents** only checked that somebody was logged in. Since a submission holds whatever people typed into the form — names, home addresses, start dates, salaries on a new-starter form — that meant any analyst at all could read every submission of every form with a direct request, whether or not Forms appeared in their module list. It now enforces module access like the rest of the folder. |
| 942 | Forms             | Fix         | **Editing a form no longer scrambles the answers people have already given it.** Until now, saving a form matched its questions up **by position** rather than by identity — so dragging a question to a new place rewrote the labels while the stored answers stayed exactly where they were. A new-starter form whose *Employee name*, *Home address* and *Starting salary* had been answered *Alice Brown / 14 Elm Road / 52000* would, after moving *Starting salary* to the top, report that person's salary as "Alice Brown" and their name as "14 Elm Road". Nothing warned you, nothing looked broken, and the submissions table went on rendering a perfectly tidy set of wrong answers — you would only catch it by remembering what somebody had actually typed. Deleting a question from the middle of a form was worse: it shifted every answer below it *and* permanently destroyed the last question's answers. Both are fixed. Every question now carries a permanent identity that travels with it, so answers stay attached to the question they were given for however much you rearrange things, and **removing a question retires it rather than deleting it** — it disappears from the form, but its column stays in the submissions view marked *removed*, because the answers people gave it are still real. This affected any form edited after it had collected responses, which for a form that is actually in use is most of them. |
| 941 | Forms             | Feature     | **Forms can now ask a question only when it's relevant.** Every question on a form used to be shown to everybody, all the time, which is why service-desk forms end up long, repetitive and half-irrelevant to whoever is filling them in. Now any question — or a whole **section** — can be given a condition: *only show this when* **"Do you need a laptop?" is "Yes"**. Answer *No* and the whole laptop block simply isn't there. Conditions can test whether an earlier answer **is / is not / contains** something, whether it was **left empty**, or whether a number is **more or less than** a value; a question can carry several conditions at once, matching **all** or **any** of them. They react as you type, on the analyst form and in the self-service portal alike. Two things are handled deliberately rather than left as traps. **A hidden question is not a required question** — otherwise a form would refuse to submit because of something the person could not see, which is the classic way this feature goes wrong — and that rule is enforced on the server, not just in the browser, so it holds even for a request that never ran our JavaScript. And an answer typed into a question that later became hidden is **not recorded**, so what you read back is what the person was actually asked. A condition can only ever depend on an **earlier** question, which is what makes a circular rule impossible to build rather than something we detect afterwards. |
| 940 | Forms             | Feature     | **Section headings, so a long form reads as the few short ones it really is.** Add a **Section heading** from the same menu as any other field and everything below it belongs to that section until the next one — *Your details*, *Equipment needed*, *Manager sign-off*. Headings render on the analyst form, in the portal and in the builder preview, and because a section owns the fields beneath it, putting a condition on the heading shows or hides **the entire group at once** rather than making you set the same rule on eight questions. The AI assistant can propose sections too, so asking it for a joiners form gets you something already grouped. A heading collects no answer, so it never appears in submissions, in the CSV export, or in the answers passed to a workflow. |
| 939 | Knowledge         | Feature     | **The knowledge base now tells you what it's missing — and writes the first draft.** Every service desk has questions it answers over and over that were never written down, and nobody notices, because each individual ticket feels too small to be worth an article. **Knowledge → Assistant** reads your closed tickets and reports back in plain English: *"I read 340 closed tickets from the last 90 days. Your knowledge base is missing six things."* Each one is a question your desk has actually answered repeatedly with nothing in the knowledge base covering it — **"Cannot open shared mailbox in Outlook — asked 14 times"** — and you can open the fourteen tickets to check before you agree. Then **Draft**, and it writes the article, streaming as it goes. **The important part is that it is allowed to say no.** A ticket that reads *"reset password, asked user to log in again"* is not an article, and a knowledge base stuffed with that is worse than an empty one — people learn it can't be trusted and stop searching it, so deflection goes *backwards*. So the assistant judges before it writes, and when a ticket only records what was done rather than what caused the problem or how it was diagnosed, it says so — and then **asks you two to four specific questions about that ticket** (*"What was the exact error in the backup job log?"*, *"How did you confirm the disk was full?"*). Answer what you can in a box, and it writes the article from your answers, which it treats as authoritative: you were there and it wasn't. It always drafts from the **most detailed** ticket in the group, never the newest — the thin tickets prove the question is worth answering, one good ticket supplies the answer. Articles come out structured as symptom, cause, resolution and how to check it worked, with **names, email addresses, phone numbers, machine names and ticket references stripped**, because these get published to a portal customers can read. Nothing is ever published automatically: every draft lands **unpublished** in your knowledge base for you to read, edit and publish yourself, and nothing unreviewed can reach the portal, the web chat or the AI answers. Once you publish, that gap stops being reported. Gaps you genuinely don't want an article for can be marked **Not needed** and stay gone even as more tickets pile into them (with a **Bring back** if you change your mind). The same thing is available from the other end too: finish a ticket and a **Write up** button appears on it, which runs exactly the same judgement — including the refusal — so you can capture something while it's fresh. Two practical notes: the assistant only speaks up once the same question has come round **three times** (adjustable, along with how far back it reads, in **Knowledge → Settings → AI**), and **finding the gaps works without any AI spend at all** — with no OpenAI key it matches on wording rather than meaning, which is cruder but still surfaces what you keep answering. Only the drafting needs a model, and it reuses the Knowledge AI key you have already set rather than asking for a second one. |
| 938 | Assets            | Feature     | **Scan asset labels without leaving FreeITSM — built for the stocktake, not the one-off.** Your phone's own camera already opens an asset label, and for looking one thing up that remains the easiest way in. It falls apart at scale: to update forty assets you leave the app, open the camera, tap the banner, edit, and repeat the whole dance forty times. **Assets → Scan** keeps the camera on the screen so the loop is scan, done, scan again. It has two modes, because what a scan should *mean* depends on the job. **Look up** is the single-asset case: point at a label and the asset opens. **Stocktake** is the one that earns its keep — choose a status and/or a location once, up front, then simply keep scanning: every asset you point at is updated as you go, with a running count and a list of what you've done. An asset that's already set the way you're setting it is **counted as seen and left alone**, so a stocktake doesn't fill five hundred histories with changes that changed nothing, and resting the camera on one label doesn't count it five times. There's an **Undo last** for the inevitable wrong laptop. It reads FreeITSM's own labels *and* the manufacturer's barcode already on most kit, so an asset you haven't tagged yet is still findable by its serial — and you can type a tag, serial or hostname when the label is damaged or the camera is blocked. On a dim shelf, the **torch** toggle appears on phones that support it. A scan gives a short buzz and blip, because in a store room you're looking at the kit, not the screen. Decoding happens **entirely on the phone** — Chrome/Android uses its built-in decoder and iPhones fall back to a bundled one that's downloaded only where it's needed, so no image of your estate is sent anywhere. Every edit goes through the same code path as a desktop edit, so asset history and the warranty calendar are updated exactly as they always were, and the same company scoping applies: a label belonging to a company you can't see is simply not recognised. ⚠️ **The camera needs an https address** — that's a browser rule, not ours, and the page says so plainly (with typing still available) rather than showing a dead black rectangle. |
| 937 | Assets            | Improvement | **Assets on a phone, round 2: the wide bits.** Round 1 (#936) made the asset list and the asset itself work on a phone. What it didn't touch was everything built as a wide table or a two-column desktop layout — and on a phone those were still the desktop screen, at desktop width. Now: the **Devices** and **Software** tabs stop being four- and three-column tables and become a readable feed — device or application name first, maker and version beneath it, status as a badge on its own line; the **History** and **Custody** trails do the same, so an asset's change history and its check-in/check-out record are actually readable rather than a table sliding off the side. The **table view**, the **dashboard**, the **settings** page and the **Servers** view are all mobile-friendly for the first time: the table view keeps its columns (they're yours to choose, so turning them into unlabelled cards would help nobody) but scrolls sideways **inside its own frame** so the page itself never moves, with the search box, buttons and count stacked for a thumb; the dashboard drops to one chart per row; settings gets a side-scrolling tab strip, full-width fields and buttons; and Servers gets two-up summary cards, scrolling filter chips, a contained table and a full-screen server detail sheet. Every one of those pages also now gets the **app shell** — the module launcher on the left and a views menu on the right — which previously only the ticket inbox and the asset list had. | 936 | Assets            | Improvement | **Assets now works on a phone.** The second module after Tickets to be brought along properly, and the one that most needs it — the whole point of the QR labels in #935 is to walk round a store room with a phone. The asset list and the asset itself no longer sit side by side fighting over a 360px screen: you get the **list**, you tap an asset and the **detail slides in** over it, and **your phone's own Back button** takes you back to the list, exactly as a native app would behave. The asset's information grid drops to a single column so values aren't truncated to nothing, the tab strip scrolls sideways instead of squashing, the action buttons wrap rather than running off the edge, and every editable field is sized so **iOS doesn't zoom the page when you tap it**. | 935 | Assets            | Feature     | **QR labels: stick a code on a laptop, scan it with your phone, and you're looking at the asset.** Every asset can now carry an **asset tag** — the number you actually write on kit (*LT0001*) — and a printable **QR label**. Open an asset and click **Print label**: you get a print-ready sheet laid out for real label stock (four common sheet sizes, from 65-per-sheet up to 12), each label carrying the QR plus the tag and hostname in plain text, because a scuffed or dirty code still has to be readable by a person. It prints straight from the browser — **no PDF tool needed** — and the codes are generated **inside your own install**, so nothing about your estate is sent to an outside QR service. The QR itself contains neither the tag nor the asset's internal number, so a photographed label gives nothing away and can't be used to guess at other assets; scanning still requires a login, and a label for a company you can't access is simply not recognised. | 934 | Tickets           | Feature     | **The ticket now tells you when a colleague is already in it.** Two analysts working the same ticket without knowing is the oldest service-desk annoyance there is: Sarah opens a ticket and starts writing about the VPN, you open the same one, see nobody has answered, and start writing your own — the customer gets two replies that may contradict each other and one of you has wasted ten minutes. It happens most on a busy morning, and most of all in Unassigned where several people triage the same list. Now, opening a ticket someone else has open shows a quiet line at the top of the reading pane — **"James Smith is also viewing this ticket"** — with their initials. If they are actually **writing a reply, a forward or a note**, it turns amber and says so, and if you then click **Reply** the composer itself warns you: *"James Smith is writing a reply to this ticket right now — check with them before you send."* It **warns and never blocks**: two people may legitimately both need to write (an escalation and a holding reply), so nothing is greyed out and nothing is locked — you're told, and the decision stays yours. It updates live in both directions, so someone starting or finishing a reply while you read appears and disappears without a refresh. Under the hood it needs nothing scheduled: an open ticket sends a heartbeat every ten seconds and anyone whose heartbeat goes quiet for thirty seconds simply stops being shown — so a closed tab, a crashed browser, a flat battery or a lost network all tidy themselves up, and nothing can leave a ghost sitting on a ticket. Presence is **not a history**: rows are overwritten by the next heartbeat and deleted freely, so this can never answer "who looked at this ticket last Tuesday". Company scoping holds exactly as it does on the ticket itself — you are never shown the name of a colleague against a ticket you couldn't open. |
| 933 | Tickets           | Feature     | **Snooze a ticket until you can actually do something with it.** Half the queue at any moment is waiting on somebody else — the user who hasn't sent the screenshot, the supplier who ships on Tuesday, the change that goes in at the weekend. Those tickets aren't work, but they sit in the inbox looking exactly like work, so every morning starts by re-reading them to re-decide they still can't be touched. **Right-click a ticket → Snooze** and pick *In 3 hours*, *This evening*, *Tomorrow*, *Next week* or an exact date and time — each option shows the real moment it means (*"Tomorrow · Wed 09:00"*), so you are never guessing, and an option stops being offered once its name would no longer be true (*This evening* disappears after 18:00). The ticket leaves every folder, and its count, and gathers in a new **Snoozed** folder listed in the order they come back. You can add a note of what you are waiting for; it shows on the ticket so a colleague finding it asleep knows why. **It comes back on its own** — waking is the clock, not a scheduled job, so a ticket returns on time even on an install with the crons switched off — and **a customer replying wakes it immediately** through any channel (email, the self-service portal, web chat, WhatsApp), because their reply is usually the very thing the snooze was waiting for. A sleeping ticket shows a banner with a **Wake now** button, and snoozing works on a whole multi-select at once. *Tomorrow* and *Next week* land on a **start of the working day** you set in **Tickets → Settings → General** (default 09:00), read in **each analyst's own timezone** so a desk spread across zones each gets their own morning. Two deliberate limits: **SLA clocks keep running** on a sleeping ticket — the customer's target is not suspended by the desk deciding to look away — and a snoozed ticket **stays findable in search and the command palette**; snoozing hides it from your folders, not from the product. Snooze is a fact about the ticket rather than a private reminder, so the whole desk sees it, with the banner naming who put it to sleep. |
| 932 | Interface         | Feature     | **Jump to anything with the command palette.** Press **⌘K** (Mac) or **Ctrl-K** (Windows/Linux) anywhere in FreeITSM to open a search-and-jump launcher — the fastest way around the app without touching the mouse. Every result deep-links to the item itself (assets are now openable by URL, `asset-management/?asset_id=…`, which they weren't before). The launcher rides on the shared header, so it's present on every analyst page automatically and follows the active theme (light/dark) with no styling of its own. |
| 931 | Contracts         | Fix         | **The Contracts left panel no longer flashes open and snaps shut on every page.** For anyone with the left panel set to "show on hover", each page load rendered the panel full-width, then — once a JavaScript lookup of the preference finished a moment later — animated it closed, producing a distracting fly-out on every click. | 929 | Self-Service      | Improvement | **Requesters can now see where their catalogue requests stand.** With approvals (#928), a submitted request that needs sign-off isn't a ticket yet — so previously it simply vanished from the customer's view until (and unless) it was approved. | 927 | Tickets           | Fix         | **Arrow-keying down the ticket list no longer scrolls the whole page.** Moving through the middle-pane list with the ↑/↓ keys keeps the selected row in view; but once you reached the bottom, the header bar was dragged off the top of the screen. The toggles are now kept at their natural size so the answer box takes the space it needs and the text is clearly visible. |
| 923 | System            | Improvement | **Demo data now covers three more modules: Learning (LMS), Workflows and Network Mapper.** The Demo Data page had no sample data for these, so evaluating them meant building content by hand. Now **Learning** seeds two authored courses — *Cyber Security Essentials* (three lessons and a real three-question quiz) and *Service Desk Induction* (three lessons); **Workflows** seeds four example automations (auto-acknowledge a new ticket, flag tickets whose subject says "urgent", broadcast a status-page incident to chat, and log every binned ticket) built on the real trigger/action engine so they open and run; and **Network Mapper** seeds a *Core Network Topology* diagram — firewall, core router and switch, five servers and three workstations — assembled from the CMDB demo's own configuration items. **Network Mapper depends on the CMDB demo**, because every node points at a real CMDB object: if CMDB hasn't been imported the import is **refused cleanly and rolled back** (naming the missing item) rather than writing a half-built diagram, so it can never leave a broken mess. All three use the existing generic importer — no import code was changed. |
| 922 | System            | Improvement | **The demo "Core Data" now seeds a realistic role-based access example.** Previously the demo created two teams (Service Desk, Escalation) and some analysts, but wired up no roles or module access — so it didn't show off how FreeITSM's permissions actually work. Importing Core Data now builds a proper out-of-the-box RBAC picture: **none of the demo analysts is an administrator**, and each has "all modules" turned **off** at their own level — their access comes entirely from their team, which is how a real install should be set up. The **Escalation Team** gets **all modules** and a matching **"Escalation Team" role holding every settings capability** (full settings access across the whole app). The **Service Desk** team is scoped to a sensible first-line subset — Watchtower, Tickets, Assets, Knowledge, Changes, Problems, Calendar, Morning checks, Service status, Wiki, Tasks and CMDB — and its matching **"Service Desk" role is deliberately blank**, so first-liners can use those modules day-to-day but change no settings. So straight after importing the demo, System → Analysts, Teams and Roles tell a coherent story you can explore and copy. Suggested by Chris18890 (#48). |
| 921 | System            | Feature     | **New debug tool: SSL / HTTPS verification check (D006).** Under **System → Debug tools** there's now a one-click diagnostic that answers "can this server actually make a certificate-verified HTTPS call, and if not, why?" — the question behind almost every mailbox, AI, webhook or sign-in connection failure. It traces the whole chain in one report: the environment (PHP, the libcurl build and its TLS backend), the global `SSL_VERIFY_PEER` switch, the `php.ini` CA settings (flagging a path that *is* set but points at a missing file — the classic silent misconfiguration), the shipped `includes/cacert.pem` (present, readable, size and certificate count, so a truncated or HTML-error-page download is obvious), **which** CA bundle actually gets used and why, and then a batch of **live certificate-verified requests to the real services the app talks to** (Microsoft Graph, Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, Slack) — distinguishing a genuine certificate failure from a plain no-network SKIP. It ends in a plain-English verdict with the one-line fix (drop a `cacert.pem` into `includes/`). Read-only, administrators-only, and prints no secrets. |
| 920 | System            | Improvement | **The setup checklist now actively *tests* HTTPS certificate verification, not just reports the setting.** Now that verification ships on (#919), the interesting failure isn't "it's switched off" — it's "it's switched on but the server has no working CA bundle", which silently breaks every outbound call (mail, AI, webhooks, sign-in). The setup page's SSL check used to go green simply because `SSL_VERIFY_PEER` was `true`, which told you nothing about whether it actually worked. It now makes a **real certificate-verified HTTPS request** through the same path the app uses and reports one of three things: **working** (green, naming the CA bundle in use), **on but cannot verify** (red — outbound HTTPS will fail, with a pointer to the CA-bundle help), or **couldn't run the test** on an air-gapped box with no outbound network (amber, inconclusive rather than a false alarm). It tells a genuine certificate problem apart from a plain no-internet box, so it never cries wolf. A companion row reports whether **`curl.cainfo` and `openssl.cafile` are set in `php.ini`** — green when configured or when relying on the shipped fallback, and amber when a path *is* set but points at a missing file (the classic silent misconfiguration). Anything short of green links straight to the HTTPS-certificates guide. |
| 919 | System            | Improvement | **HTTPS certificate verification is now secure by default, and just works.** FreeITSM makes a lot of outbound HTTPS calls — Microsoft Graph and other mailboxes, AI providers, single sign-on, Intune and vCenter syncs, webhooks, share emails, password-reset mail. Verifying the certificate on those calls is what stops FreeITSM being tricked into handing your ticket data to an impostor (a "man-in-the-middle"). The shipped default in `config.php` was `SSL_VERIFY_PEER = false` — verification **off** — because on a stock Windows/WAMP install PHP has no list of trusted certificate authorities, so switching it on would make every one of those calls fail. That trade-off is now gone: **FreeITSM bundles its own CA certificate list** (`includes/cacert.pem`) and points cURL at it automatically when the server has none configured, so verification is **on by default and works out of the box** — no `php.ini` surgery required. Raised by Chris18890 (#49). **The confusing per-module "Verify SSL" tick-boxes are gone.** They had crept onto several settings pages (the shared AI provider panel used by Knowledge, CMDB, Workflows, Forms, Problems and LMS; the Intune connector; the RFP Builder) and behaved inconsistently — the AI one was ANDed with the global switch, so on a typical install it showed *unchecked* and appeared not to save, while Intune and RFP verified independently. There is now **one setting that governs everything**: `SSL_VERIFY_PEER` in `config.php`, applied through a single shared helper (`sslApplyCurl`). The Docker image, which uses its own `docker/config.php`, carries the same secure default and loads the shared helper (its Debian base already provides a system CA bundle, so it needs no shipped cert). Webhooks continue to **always** verify, by design — they carry record data to third parties over the public internet, so there is deliberately no off switch for them. **⚠️ One thing to check after upgrading:** if you sync from a **vCenter/ESXi** host using a **self-signed certificate**, those calls verified nothing before and will now be checked — add that host's certificate to `cacert.pem` (the in-app HTTPS help page explains how) or the sync will fail. The same applies to any internal service presenting a private certificate. |
| 918 | System            | Fix         | **The default timezone in `config.php` now matches the rest of the app.** A fresh `config.php` set PHP's fallback timezone to `America/New_York`, while everything the app actually seeds — the default SLA business-hours calendar, the timezone picker in Tickets settings — defaults to `Europe/London`. That single line was the odd one out. It now reads `Europe/London` too, so a new install is internally consistent out of the box. This only affects bare `date()` calls where no zone is given: stored datetimes are UTC and displayed in each user's own timezone (Settings → Preferences), and SLA clocks run against their calendar's zone, so nothing that was correct before changes. Raised by Chris18890 (#49). |
| 917 | Tickets           | Improvement | **The in-app help now covers the new analyst tools.** Tickets → Help has a new section, **Working faster**, bringing together canned responses, selecting several tickets at once, merging duplicates, splitting a ticket that holds two jobs, and undoing both — with the keyboard map, the settings involved, and the practical tips that are easy to miss (name a template for the situation not its wording; give a split ticket a proper subject). |
| 916 | Tickets           | Feature     | **Undo a merge.** A merged-away ticket now offers **Undo merge** on its banner: the messages, notes and logged time it brought with it come back, and it reopens **exactly as it was** — including its original status and closed date, so a ticket that had been resolved before somebody merged it does not come back mistakenly "Open". If the merge produced HTML snapshot attachments, those are removed along with their files; if the merge created a brand-new ticket (the *new reference* setting), that ticket goes to the trash once the last ticket has been taken back out of it. **What it deliberately does not do is rewind the other ticket.** Replies written on the surviving ticket since the merge stay there — they were written to that conversation, and dragging them somewhere else would not be a reversal. The confirmation says so before you commit. Merges made before FreeITSM started recording which messages moved cannot be undone automatically, and the button is hidden rather than offered and then refused. |
| 915 | Tickets           | Feature     | **Undo a split.** Split a ticket by mistake, or split at the wrong message? The split banner now offers **Undo split**: the messages come straight back, the marker left in the conversation disappears, and the ticket that was created goes to the trash. Other tools are notably weak here — Freshdesk publishes a support article titled *"Can I unsplit a ticket?"* because people keep asking. **It refuses rather than guesses.** If anyone has replied on the new ticket, added a note, or logged time against it, the undo is declined with an explanation naming exactly what is in the way — because that reply was written about a different problem, and dragging it back is not a reversal but a second mistake. FreeITSM now also **records exactly which messages moved** on every split *and* every merge, which is what makes an undo possible at all: a count alone would leave it guessing which messages to send back. **Splits and merges performed before this release cannot be undone automatically** — there is no record of which messages moved, and guessing would scatter a conversation permanently. Unmerge is not built yet, but the recording that makes it possible is now in place. |
| 914 | Tickets           | Feature     | **Split a ticket when a customer raises a second, unrelated thing.** "My printer is offline… oh, and my monitor keeps flickering" is two pieces of work sharing one SLA clock, one status and one owner — and whichever gets fixed second looks late. Hover any message in the conversation and click **Split**: that message moves to a brand-new ticket, optionally taking every **newer** message with it. The dialog lists exactly what will move before you commit, and lets you give the new ticket a proper subject (it defaults to the moved message's, which is usually a "RE:" of the *old* problem). The messages genuinely **move** rather than being copied — a copy would leave the same customer message on two tickets for two people to answer — and the original keeps a marker in the conversation showing where they went, so the thread never silently jumps from Tuesday to Friday. Both tickets stay open, linked as **Related**, each with a banner pointing at the other. FreeITSM refuses to move *every* message, since that would leave the original an empty shell holding a reference the customer still has. |
| 913 | Tickets           | Fix         | **Ticket action buttons no longer run off the side of the screen.** The *Request feedback* button is now just **Feedback**, matching the one-word style of the rest of the toolbar. More importantly, the cause was found and fixed: the reading pane was a flex item using the browser's default minimum width, so instead of scrolling it **grew to fit its widest content** — one bounce email containing a very long unbroken address stretched the pane to over 5,000 pixels and pushed the toolbar, and everything else, off the right of the screen. The pane now keeps to its share of the window and long content wraps inside it, and the toolbar wraps onto a second line rather than overflowing. Measured on a real ticket: 5,234px wide before, 702px after, with all eight buttons reachable. The buttons themselves are also **noticeably more compact** — around half the previous padding — so the row reads as a toolbar and fits in far less space. Phones and tablets keep their larger touch targets. |
| 912 | Tickets           | Feature     | **Merge tickets — with an AI briefing of what everyone asked and what has been done.** When two people report the same printer, or a monitoring system opens forty tickets for one outage, select them in the inbox and **right-click → Merge**. The conversations come together into one ticket, and — if you have an AI provider configured — FreeITSM reads the combined thread and writes a short briefing: **what has been asked** (who reported what) and **what has been done** (what the desk has already tried or promised). It streams in as you watch, you can edit it, and it saves as an internal note that is never shown to the requester. Merging works perfectly well without AI; the briefing is a bonus, not the mechanism. **How merging behaves is your choice**, on a new **Tickets → Settings → Merge behaviour** tab. The reference can either stay with **one of the existing tickets** (the others close and point at it) or become a **brand-new ticket** that all of them fold into. The original conversations can be **moved into the merged ticket**, **moved and also attached as HTML files**, or **attached as HTML files only**. **Nothing is ever deleted.** A merged-away ticket keeps its own reference forever, stays searchable, and shows a banner saying where it went — so "whatever happened to ABC?" always has an answer. Crucially, **a customer replying to an old email about ABC still reaches you**: FreeITSM follows the merge and lands their reply on the live ticket instead of a closed one nobody is watching. |
| 911 | System            | Fix         | **The Preferences page was completely broken and served a blank error.** `system/preferences/index.php` called `htmlspecialchars()` with no argument when setting the page's `lang` attribute, which in PHP 8 is a fatal `ArgumentCountError` — so the entire page died before rendering a single control, and nobody could change their language, timezone, theme, toast position or left-panel settings. It returned **HTTP 200** with a 408-byte error body, which is why nothing flagged it. Found while adding a new preference to the same page. |
| 910 | Tickets           | Feature     | **Select several tickets at once, and act on all of them.** The inbox now works the way Outlook and File Explorer do: **click** selects one, **Ctrl+click** toggles tickets in and out one by one, **Shift+click** takes a whole block, and **Ctrl+Shift+click** extends a block without losing what you already picked. No checkboxes. It works from the keyboard too — **↑/↓** to move, **Shift+↑/↓** to extend, **Ctrl+↑/↓** to move the cursor without changing the selection, **Space** to toggle the row under it, **Ctrl+A** for everything listed and **Escape** to clear. With more than one selected, the **right-click menu acts on the whole selection** — so status, priority, department, type and assignee can all be set for fifty tickets in two clicks — and you can **drag the whole selection onto a folder** to re-triage it, or onto Trash — the drag shows a **stack of pages carrying a count badge**, so it is obvious you are moving twelve tickets and not the one under the pointer. There is also a **Delete** action with a counted confirmation (it is the same soft delete, so Restore is the undo). Because there is no single right answer for what the screen should do while several are selected, **it is your choice**: a new *Selecting several tickets* setting in the account menu → Preferences offers a **summary panel** listing what you picked with the actions on it (the default), **keeping the ticket you opened on screen** with a reminder that an action will hit all of them, or a **compact bar above the list**. Bulk changes run through exactly the same service as changing one ticket, so audit trails, SLA clocks, notification emails and workflow triggers all behave identically — and each ticket gets its own audit entry recording its real previous value. |
| 909 | Tickets           | Feature     | **Canned responses: save a reply once, then insert it with one click.** Analysts retype the same handful of replies every day — the password-reset confirmation, the request for more detail, the "escalated to our supplier" note. Templates are **rich text** (the same editor as the reply itself) and support the **same `[merge_code]` placeholders as the automated email templates** — `[requester_first_name]`, `[ticket_reference]`, `[analyst_name]` and the rest — resolved against the real ticket at the moment you insert them. There are **two kinds**: shared team templates, curated in **Tickets → Settings → Reply templates** under a new permission, and an analyst's **own private ones**, saved straight from the reply window with **Save draft as template** and needing no permission at all — so having a personal template does not depend on someone granting you settings access. Your private templates are visible only to you; not even an administrator's picker lists them. | 908 | System            | Improvement | **The application root is tidy, and the login page has one proper URL.** The root folder held fifteen loose PHP files; the login page was reachable at three different addresses, one of which (`/login/index.php`) served a half-broken page with the logo missing — an accident of Apache's MultiViews option mapping URLs onto files by guesswork (and in Docker, which has no MultiViews, `/login` didn't work at all). The auth pages now live in `auth/`, the CSAT survey with its module at `tickets/csat/`, the Intune background workers in `scripts/`, leaving the root with just `index.php` and the config files. **`/login` is now the one canonical login URL** everywhere, including Docker: the old `login.php` links (there are ~100 across the app, plus everyone's bookmarks) permanently redirect to it, form posts still work, and `/forgot-password`, `/reset-password` and `/csat` got the same treatment. Nothing external changes: **CSAT survey links in already-sent emails keep working forever**, password-reset emails keep working, and the **OAuth callback URLs registered in Azure and Google are byte-for-byte unchanged** — the files moved but the URLs are rewritten internally, so there is nothing to re-register. Every move is documented on the new **Root folder tidy** wiki page. |
| 907 | Documentation     | Improvement | **The project README is now a proper landing page.** It had grown to over 1,500 lines of developer reference — directory trees, endpoint tables, database schemas — which buried the answer to "what is this and how do I try it?" and made the repo's front page off-putting for new visitors. It is now ~130 lines: what FreeITSM is, screenshots, a Docker quick start, the module list, highlights, and links into the documentation wiki. **Nothing was lost**: every fact the old README held that the wiki lacked was first merged into the right wiki page (615 lines added across 33 pages — the full email-threading design onto Tickets, the directory layout and dev checklists onto Architecture, per-endpoint tables onto API Reference, the icon library onto Network Mapper, Branding and the landing-page/search internals onto System, and more).
